My idea for the 2-D case is as follows. Let S_{m,n} be the (n,m)-"cube", ie, the collection of all pairs (x,y) with x in 0,1,...,m and y in 0, ..., n, but excluding (0,0), and let T_{m,n} be the boundary (all such points with x in {0,m} and y in {0,n}. So T_{m,n} has 2m+2n-1 points. Now consider a collection of "hyperplanes" (lines) not containing (0,0) and covering all points  in S_{m,n}. We want to show that there are at least m+n lines needed. Now, if there is a line that covers more than two points from the boundary, then it is a boundary line, hence one of the two boundary lines through (m,n). In that case, the other lines lines cover S_{m,n-1} or S_{m-1,n}, and the desired result follows by induction. On the other hand, if all lines cover at most two boundary points, then there are at least (2m+2n-1)/2 lines, hence at least n+m lines.

Probably yes... However, you need to adjust your notation slightly: to cover the cube with $ \{0,1,\ldots,n+m\}$ without the cube with $ \{0,1,\ldots,m\}$ , you need(?) at least $ 3n$ planes. The CN argument can be modified to show that you need at least $ 3n-3m$ planes, which is probably not sharp unless $ m=0$ (the original problem). More generally, to cover an $ n_{1}\times \cdots \times n_{k}$ grid without an $ \ell_{1}\times \cdots \times \ell_{k}$ subgrid, one needs at least $ \sum_{i=1}^{k}\max (n_{i}-2\ell_{i}+2, 0)$ hyperplanes. Perhaps this bound may be improved to $ \sum_{i=1}^{k}(n_{i}-\ell_{i}+1)$ in the case that each $ n_{i}> \ell_{i}> 0$ , but I can't show this at the moment. Let me demonstrate the version with $ 3n$ and $ 3$ dimensions (the general case being only notationally different). Let $ a_{i}x+b_{i}y+c_{i}z = d_{i}$ be the planes, $ 1 \leq i \leq s$ ; and suppose $ s < 3n-3m$ . Let $ P(x,y,z) : = \prod_{i=1}^{s}(a_{i}x+b_{i}y+c_{i}z-d_{i})$ , and let $ Q(x,y,z)$ be the polynomial, of degree $ \leq m$ in each variable $ x,y,z$ , obtained from $ P(x,y,z)$ modulo the relations $ \prod_{j=0}^{m}(x-j) = \prod_{j=0}^{m}(y-j) = \prod_{j=0}^{m}(z-j) = 0$ (that is, we replace successively each $ x^{m+1},y^{m+1}, z^{m+1}$ with linear combinations of smaller powers using these relations, until there is no monomial left with partial degree $ > m$ ). By construction, $ Q(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z)$ for $ x,y,z \in{0,\ldots,m}$ . Let as well $ R(x,y,z)$ be the polynomial, again of degree $ \leq m$ in each variable, obtained from the polynomial $ S(x,y,z) : = \prod_{j=m+1}^{n+m}(x-j)(y-j)(z-j)$ modulo these same relations. Once again, $ S(x,y,z)$ and $ R(x,y,z)$ take the same values on $ \{0,\ldots,m \}^{3}$ . Consider the polynomial $ T(x,y,z) : = P(x,y,z) R(x,y,z)-Q(x,y,z)S(x,y,z)$ . The first summand, $ PR$ , has total degree $ s+\deg{R}= s+3m < 3n = \deg{S}\leq \deg{QS}$ , and in $ QS$ the partial degrees in $ x,y,z$ are all $ \leq n+m$ . The contradiction follows from the combinatorial nullstellensatz, since $ T(x,y,z)$ vanishes identically on $ \{0,1,\ldots,n+m\}^{3}$ . Absolutely this problem is a poor choice by the Committe. The more I think about a combinatorial approach, the more I realize that this is totally not a combinatorial problem: it was *invented* (i.e. discovered) in 1993 (Alon - Furedi) as an application of the (algebraic) polynomial method of N. Alon, and I don't believe that it has a combinatorial meaning, at least in the general case (for the 3-D case the proposers may have found a combinatorial solution, I don't know yet; but I doubt it would generalize. I actually find it quite likely that all known proofs are algebraic!). Those planes and their incidence with the lattice points have absolutely no "natural" combinatorial meaning, which is why this problem is so difficult to organize combinatorially *ad hoc*. Some people call such problems *algebro-combinatorial*, some put them in the realm of *combinatorial geometry* (both are reasonable: the known solutions are algebraic, while the objects of study, planes and integral points on them, are geometric)... And some would call such problems *artificial*. But [or *moreover*] such questions abound in the literature on combinatorial geometry/combinatorial group theory/algebraic combinatorics. This is not a generalization, but a (more interesting, actually) finite analog: for a finite abelian group $ A$ with identity $ 0$ , what is the minimal number of cosets [of subgroups $ H < A$ ] whose union is $ A \setminus \{0\}$ ? For the answer and proof, and similar questions, here is an interesting article for the interested reader: http://www.citebase.org/fulltext?format=application%2Fpdf&identifier=oai%3AarXiv.org%3Amath%2F0411244 . **2.** Above was proposed the following generalization for which I proved a weaker version: *To cover the cube with $ \{0,1,\ldots,n+m\}$ without the cube with $ \{0,1,\ldots,m\}$ , we need at least 3n planes.* I showed that we need at least $ 3(n-m)$ planes. But actually, the proof shows more: *Suppose that: (1) we have covered all points of the cube with $ \{0,1,\ldots,n+m\}$ except possibly some points of the cube with $ \{0,1,\ldots,m\}$ ; and (2) we have **not** covered at least one point of the cube with $ \{0,1,\ldots,m\}$ . Then we have used at least $ 3(n-m)$ hyperplanes. Similarly for the obvious generalization.* Indeed, all that we used about the polynomial $ Q$ constructed in the proof that it was not the zero polynomial. This follows from the assumption that $ Q$ does not vanish on the cube with $ \{0,1,\ldots,m\}$ . But it suffices to assume that $ Q$ does not vanish at just one point to reach the conclusion. Again, this is probably not sharp in general. That said, I believe one can prove the sharp result conjectured by mszew as follows. I use the notation for my proof of the special case above. Instead of constructing $ Q$ and $ R$ as we did, construct ("kinds of inverses") polynomials $ Q, R$ of partial degrees all $ \leq m$ as follows: (i) $ PQ$ takes the value $ 1$ on the cube with $ \{0,1,\ldots,m\}$ (here we use with full force that $ P$ does not vanish on this cube, i.e. that the union of our planes is exactly the cube with $ \{0,1,\ldots,n+m\}$ minus the cube with $ \{0,1,\ldots,m\}$ ); and $ RS$ as well takes the value $ 1$ identically on the cube with $ \{0,1,\ldots,m\}$ . Then $ R$ is a concrete polynomial (with concrete coefficients independent of the given covering), because $ S : = \prod_{j = m+1}^{n+m}(x-j)(y-j)(z-j)$ is. And I think we may show that the coefficient of $ (xyz)^{m}$ in $ R(x,y,z)$ is nonzero. If this is the case, then we may apply CN to the polynomial $ PQ-RS$ and conclude the proof! Thus, modulo my computational claim, we have two different generalizations of the initial problem, still in dimension $ 3$ and with cubes rather than general parallelepipeds! But the generalizations to such questions are countless.

Here is a proof that looks simpler that the official solution, even though it uses the same principle. It is similar to a 'A short proof of Combinatorial Nullstellensatz' given by Mateusz Michalek. I'd be really grateful if someone could check this for mistakes.

Let  $n_1, \ldots, n_d \in \mathbb{N}$ . Let
            \[S(n_1, \ldots, n_d) = \{(x_1, \ldots, x_d)\, | \, 0 \leq x_i \leq n_i,\, x_1 + \ldots + x_d > 0\}.\]
            Consider a polynomial  $P$  that *solves*  $S(n_1, \ldots, n_d)$ , that is,  $P(x_1, \ldots, x_d) = 0$  for all  $(x_1, \ldots, x_d) \in S$  and  $P(0, \ldots, 0) \neq 0$ . We show by induction that  $\deg(P) \geq n_1 + \ldots + n_d$ . Assume w.l.o.g. that  $n_1 > 0$ . Apply polynomial division to write
            \[P = P'(x_1 - n_1) + R,\]
            such that  $\deg(R) \leq \deg(P)$  and  $R$  does not contain  $x_1$ . It is easy to see that 
            \[R(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = R(n_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n) = P(n_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n).\]
            This means that  $R(x_1, \ldots, x_d) = 0$  for all  $(x_1, \ldots, x_d) \in S(n_1, \ldots, n_d) \cup \{0\}$ . Clearly then  $P'$  solves  $S(n_1 - 1, \ldots, n_d)$ . By induction we are done since
            \[\deg(P) \geq \deg(P - R) = \deg(P'(x_1 - n_1)) = \deg(P') + 1.\]

Note that my solution directly solves the more general problem given here, in the generalized form: Suppose that: (1) we have covered all points of the cube with $ \{0,1,\ldots,n+m\}$ except possibly some points of the cube with $ \{0,1,\ldots,m\}$ ; and (2) we have not covered at least one point of the cube with $ \{0,1,\ldots,m\}$ . This is the Field Medalist :o

We claim the answer  $3n$ . As an example take a union of planes  $x+y+z=c$  for  $c=1,2,\dots ,3n.$ Assume FTSOC that planes  $a_ix+b_iy+c_iz+d_i=0$  for  $i=1,2,\dots ,k<3n$  cover  $S;$  consider polynomial   $$ P(x,y,z)=(x+y+z)\prod_{i=1}^{k} (a_ix+b_iy+c_iz+d_i) $$   and set  $\mathcal A=\left \{ 0,1,2,\dots ,n\right \} .$  Since  $d_i\neq 0,$  at least one monom  $x^py^qz^r$  of  $P$  (with  $p+q+r\leq k+1$ ) has a nonzero coefficient, hence by the Combinatorial Nullstellensatz there exist  $s_{1,2,3}\in \mathcal A$  such that  $P(s_1,s_2,s_3)\neq 0.$  Since  $P(0,0,0)=0,$  we get the obvious contradiction, as desired.

The answer is  $3n$ . For the construction, use the planes  $x=1, 2, \ldots, n$ ,  $y=1, 2, \ldots, n$ , and  $z=1, 2, \ldots, n$ . Now we show that no number of planes  $k<3n$  works. Assume for contradiction that a configuration with  $k<3n$  planes exists. Let these planes be  $a_ix + b_iy + c_iz + d_i=0$  for  $1 \le i \le k$ . Define \[ f(x, y, z) = \prod_{i=1}^k (a_ix + b_iy + c_iz + d_i) \ \text{and} \ g(x, y, z) =  \prod_{i=1}^n (x-i) \prod_{i=1}^n (y-i) \prod_{i=1}^n (z-i).  \] 
Furthermore, let \[ P(x, y, z) = f(x, y, z)-\frac{f(0, 0, 0)}{g(0, 0, 0)} g(x, y, z). \] Note that  $P$  vanishes on  $\{0, 1, \ldots, n\}^3$ . However, the coefficent of  $x^ny^nz^n$  in  $P$  is  $-\frac{f(0, 0, 0)}{g(0, 0, 0)}$  which is nonzero, so the combinatorial Nullstellensatz yields a contradiction, which completes the proof.

Answer is  $3n$ . FTSOC assume that there are  $p < 3n$  planes.
Then let polynomials  $P_1(x, y, z) = \prod_{i=1}^p (a_ix + b_iy + c_iz + 1)$  where  $a_ix + b_iy + c_iz + 1 = 0$  determines the planes in question.
Then let  $P_2(x, y, z) = \prod_{i=1}^k (x-i)\prod_{i=1}^k (y-i)\prod_{i=1}^k (z-i)$ . Note that both  $P_1$  and  $P_2$  vanish completely on  $S$ . Clearly both  $P_1(0, 0, 0)$  and  $P_2(0, 0, 0)$  are nonzero. So then  $P(x, y, z) = P_1(x, y, z) - \frac{P_1(0,0,0)}{P_2(0,0,0)} \cdot P_2(x,y,z)$  has total degree of less than  $3n$ , and it vanishes completely over  $T^3$  where  $T = (0, 1, \dots, n)$ . Then Combinatorial Nullstellensatz gives us that  $P(x,y,z)$  has no nonzero terms, which is a contradiction as  $P_1$  and  $P_2$  both have a nonzero ending coefficient of  $1$  and  $(-1)^n \cdot n!$  respectively so we have proved the bound.
For our construction, just take  $3n$  planes, split into  $n$  groups of planes that are parallel to the  $XY$ ,  $XZ$ , and  $YZ$  planes passing through  $(0, 0, 0)$ . It is easy to arrange the planes so that they pass through all of  $S$  so we are done.

The answer is  $3n$  planes. Taking  $x+y+z = i$  for each  $1 \leq i \leq 3n$  gives a construction.

Suppose for the sake of contradiction that there are  $k<3n$  planes, and let the planes have equations  $a_ix+b_iy+c_iz + 1=0$  for each  $1 \leq i \leq k$ . Consider the two polynomials 
\begin{align*}
P(x, y, z) &= \left(\prod_{i=1}^n (x-i)\right)\left(\prod_{i=1}^n (y-i)\right)\left(\prod_{i=1}^n (z-i)\right) 
Q(x, y, z) &= \prod_{i=1}^k \left(a_i x + b_iy+c_iz + 1\right).
\end{align*}
Then  $P(0, 0, 0)$  and  $Q(0, 0, 0)$  are both nonzero; in particular, there exists a  $\lambda$  such that  $P-\lambda Q$  evaluates to zero at  $(0, 0, 0)$ . Then this polynomial evaluates to zero on all points in  $\{0, 1, \dots, n\}^3$ . But the degree of  $Q$  is  $k < 3n$ , so  $P-\lambda Q$  has a nonzero  $x^ny^nz^n$  term inherited from  $P$ . This contradicts the combinatorial nullstellensatz.

stem_md:
Prove that there are infinitely many positive integers  $ n$  such that  $ n^{2} \plus{} 1$  has a prime divisor greater than  $ 2n \plus{} \sqrt {2n}$ .

*Author: Kestutis Cesnavicius, Lithuania*
solution_md:
I realized that I had written this solution up around five months ago, why not post it; the same solution as some other on the thread except with more of the details provided for motivating the solution, similar to <details><summary>problem I solved since this write-up</summary>USAMO 2006, P3</details>.
<details><summary>Solution</summary>$\textbf{Lemma 1:}$  
It suffices to find infinitely many primes  $p$  such that there exists some  $n \in \mathbb{N}$  such that  $p \mid n^2+1$  and  $n < \frac{p-1}{2}-\sqrt{\frac{p}{4}}$ .  $\textbf{Proof)}$  
Notice that for each prime  $p$ , there is at most one  $n \in \mathbb{N}$  satisfying the condition because  $x^2+1$  has at most two roots in  $\mathbb{F}_{p}[x]$  which come in a pair  $n,p-n$ , one of which is at least  $\frac{p}{2}$  and consequently does not satisfy the condition. 
Therefore, if we have that there are infinitely many primes  $p$  with  $n \in \mathbb{N}$  satisfying the condition for said prime and take  $A$  to be the set of all such primes, then we can consider the map  $f: A \to \mathbb{N}$  such that  $p \mid f(p)^2+1$  and  $f(p)< \frac{p-1}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{p}{4}}$ . 
Moreover,  $f$  is injective because if  $f(p) = f(q)$  with  $p \neq q$ ,   $$ n^2+1 \geq pq > (2n+\sqrt{2n})^2 $$   which is not possible. 
As  $A$  has infinitely many elements the image of  $f$  must be infinite, then taking any element of the image, notice that   $$ p>2(\frac{p-1}{2}-\sqrt{\frac{p}{4}})+\sqrt{2(\frac{p-1}{2}-\sqrt{\frac{p}{4}})}>2f(p)+\sqrt{2f(p)} $$   meaning that each element of the infinite image of  $f$  satisfies the condition as  $f(p)^2+1$  always has a prime divisor that is at least  $2f(p)+\sqrt{2f(p)}$ , as desired.  $\blacksquare$  

We shall now prove that there are indeed infinitely many prime numbers  $p$  such that there is an  $n \in \mathbb{N}$  satisfying the condition which by  $\textbf{Lemma 1}$  imply the problem. 

Take a prime  $p$  such that  $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$  and  $p \equiv 2 \pmod{5}$  of which there are infinitely many by Dirichlet's Theorem.  $\textbf{Lemma 2:}$  
There exists some  $n \in \mathbb{N}$  such that  $p \mid n^2+1$   $\textbf{Proof)}$  
Let  $g$  be a primitive root  $\pmod{p}$  and let  $n = g^{\frac{p-1}{4}}$ . 
Then  $n \in \mathbb{N}$  and   $$ n^2 \equiv (g^{\frac{p-1}{4}})^2 \equiv -1 \pmod{p} $$   which immediately gives us the existence of an integer  $n$  such that  $p \mid n^2+1$ .  $\textbf{Lemma 3:}$  
There exists some  $n \in \mathbb{N}$  such that  $p \mid n^2+1$  and  $p > 2n+\sqrt{2n}$   $\textbf{Proof)}$  
Notice by  $\textbf{Lemma 2}$  that there exists some  $n \in \mathbb{N}$  such that  $p \mid n^2+1$ , similarly, notice that  $p \mid (p-n)^2+1$ , therefore we can in fact find some  $n \in \{0,..,\frac{p-1}{2}\}$  such that  $p \mid n^2+1$ . 
Naturally, we may write  $n = \frac{p-1}{2}-k$  for some  $k \in \{0,...,\frac{p-1}{2}\}$ . 
Then   $$ -1 \equiv (\frac{p-1}{2}-k)^2 \equiv k^2+k+\frac{1}{4} \pmod{p} $$  Therefore   $$ p \mid k^2+k+\frac{3p+5}{4} $$   because  $\frac{5}{4} \equiv \frac{3p+5}{4} \pmod{p}$  and  $4 \mid 3p+5$  as  $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ .  $\blacksquare$  $\textbf{Claim:}$   $k > \sqrt{\frac{p}{4}}$   $\textbf{Proof)}$  
Assume for the sake of contradiction that  $k \leq \sqrt{\frac{p}{4}}$ . 
Then, notice that   $$ 2p> p+\frac{5}{4}+\sqrt{\frac{p}{4}} =  (\sqrt{\frac{p}{4}})^2+\sqrt{\frac{p}{4}}+\frac{3p+5}{4}\geq k^2+k+\frac{3p+5}{4} $$  meaning that  $p = k^2+k+\frac{3p+5}{4}$  as  $p \mid k^2+k+\frac{3p+5}{4}$ . 
Therefore we have that  $p = 4k^2+4k+5$ , yet,   $$ 2 \equiv p \equiv -k^2-k \equiv 0,3,4 \pmod{5} $$   which is a clear contradiction, as desired.  $\blacksquare$  

Then, notice that   $$ n = \frac{p-1}{2}-k < \frac{p-1}{2}-\sqrt{\frac{p}{4}} $$  which by  $\textbf{Lemma 1}$  suffices.  $\blacksquare$</details>

Fix a prime  $ p$  of the form  $ 20m\plus{}1$ . There are two solutions to the congruence  $ n^2 \equiv \minus{}1 \pmod{p}$ , one of them is less then  $ \frac{p\minus{}1}{2}$  and one is greater. Let  $ \frac{p\minus{}1}{2}\minus{}k$  be the smaller one ( $ k>0$ ). Now we want find a lower bound for the  $ k$ , let's see what do we need. Take for simplicity  $ \frac{p\minus{}1}{2} \equal{} a$ . We want to have: $ 2(a\minus{}k) \plus{} \sqrt{2(a\minus{}k)} \leq p\minus{}1$ 
or $ a\minus{}k \plus{} \sqrt{\frac{a\minus{}k}{2}} \leq a$ 
which is equivalent to $ a \leq 2k^2 \plus{} k$ 
and finally $ p \leq 4k^2 \plus{} 2k \plus{} 1$ .

Ok, now we see that  $ (\frac{p\minus{}1}{2} \minus{} k)^2 \equiv \minus{}1 \pmod{p}$  is equivalent to  $ (2k\plus{}1)^2 \equiv \minus{}4 \pmod{p}$ . But  $ p\minus{}4 \equiv 3 \pmod{5}$ , so it's not a square. Of course  $ (2k\plus{}1)^2 \not \equal{} 2p\minus{}4$  since the parity is different. Therefore  $ (2k\plus{}1)^2 \geq 3p\minus{}4$ , i.e.  $ 4k^2\plus{}4k \plus{} 5 \geq 3p$  and it's clear that the desired inequality is satisfied.

Note that for any prime  $ p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ , we can always choose some  $ \alpha \in \{ 0, \ldots, \frac{p\minus{}3}{2} \}$  such that  $ \left(\frac{p\minus{}1}{2} \minus{} \alpha \right)^2 \equiv \minus{}1 \pmod{p}$ . Denote  $ m \equal{} \frac{p\minus{}1}{2} \minus{} \alpha$ . This problem then becomes equivalent to choosing a suitable  $ p$ , with corresponding  $ \alpha$ , such that  $ p > 2m \plus{} \sqrt{2m}$ . We check that \[ p > p\minus{}1 \minus{} 2\alpha \plus{} \sqrt{p\minus{}1\minus{}2\alpha} \Leftrightarrow 2\alpha \plus{} 1 > \sqrt{p\minus{}1\minus{}2\alpha} \Leftrightarrow 4\alpha^2 \plus{} 6\alpha \plus{} 2\minus{}p >0.\] Solving this quadratic inequality, since we assumed  $ \alpha \geq 0$ , this is equivalent to \[ \alpha > \dfrac{\minus{}6\plus{}\sqrt{36\plus{}16(p\minus{}2)}}{8} \equal{} \dfrac{\minus{}3\plus{}\sqrt{4p\plus{}1}}{4}.\]

Hence, if  $ \alpha > \dfrac{\minus{}3\plus{}\sqrt{4p\plus{}1}}{4}$ , then we are done. Suppose not, then we have  $ 0 \leq \alpha \leq \dfrac{\minus{}3\plus{}\sqrt{4p\plus{}1}}{4}$ . Note that  $ 4m^2 \equal{} (p\minus{}1\minus{}2\alpha)^2 \equiv (2\alpha\plus{}1)^2 \pmod{p}$ . By the bounds on  $ \alpha$ , we get  $ 0 \leq (2\alpha\plus{}1)^2 \leq \left( \dfrac{\sqrt{4p\plus{}1} \minus{} 1}{2} \right)^2$ . Now, by assumption,  $ 4m^2 \equiv \minus{}4 \pmod{p}$ , so if  $ \left( \dfrac{\sqrt{4p\plus{}1} \minus{} 1}{2} \right)^2 < p\minus{}4$ , we get a contradiction. Solving this inequality, this is equilavent to  $ p>20$ .

Therefore, if  $ p$  is sufficiently large (i.e.  $ p>20$ ) and  $ p\equiv 1 \pmod{p}$ , we can always find some  $ m$  such that  $ p|(m^2\plus{}1)$  and  $ p > 2m \plus{} \sqrt{2m}$ .

If solution of the problem consists only of two simple steps – it isn’t third.**My solution.** Consider the set of numbers  $ S\equal{}$ { $ p \in \mathbb{P} | p \equiv 1 \mod 4, p \not \equal{} 5,13$ }. 
For every  $ p \in S$  let us define set of positive integers  $ N_p$  such that  $ n \in N_p \leftrightarrow p|n^2\plus{}1$  and  $ n_p$  - the minimal of them.
It’s easily seen that  $ n_p<p$  and also  $ n_p<\frac{p}{2}$  else we can take  $ p\minus{}n_p$  instead of   $ n_p$ .
Let  $ k_p$  be  $ p\minus{}2n_p$ . Then  $ k_p^2\plus{}4\equal{}(p\minus{}2n_p)^2\plus{}4 \equiv 4(n_p^2\plus{}1) \equiv 0 \mod p$ , hence  $ k^2\plus{}4>\equal{}p$ . 
Let us notice that  $ k_p>4$ . Really, if this isn’t true then there are only two variants:  $ k_p\equal{}1$  and  $ k_p\equal{}3$  since  $ k_p$  is odd. If  $ k_p\equal{}1$  then  $ p|1^2\plus{}4$  and  $ p\equal{}5$  - contr; if  $ k_p\equal{}3$  then  $ p|3^2\plus{}4$  and  $ p\equal{}13$  -contr. 
So we have  $ k_p^2\plus{}k_p>k_p\plus{}4 \ge p$ , therefore  $ p\minus{}k_p\plus{}\sqrt{p\minus{}k_p}<p$  or  $ 2n_p\plus{}\sqrt{2n_p}<p$ . Since  $ |S|\equal{}\infty$  then there are infinitely many different integers  $ n_p$  such that  $ p \in S$ , so we are done.
Evidently it’s possible to estimate this value better. For example if we take the set  $ T\equal{}$ { $ p \in \mathbb{P} | p \equiv 1 \mod 4, p \equiv 1 \mod 5$ } then for every  $ p \in T$   $ p\minus{}4$  isn’t square of integer and hence  $ k_p^2\plus{}4 \ge 5p$ .

Here's a proof for  $cn\log n$  for some  $c>0$ . (I read this in a handout by Géza Kós a while ago.)

Suppose for a contradiction that for large enough  $n$ , the largest prime divisor of  $n^2+1$  is at most  $cn\log n$  for some  $c>0$ .

As written in the ISL, we estimate the product  $P=P(N)=\prod_{n=1}^N (n^2+1)$  by investigating its prime factorization. This product can be written as  $$ P=2^{v_2(P)}\cdot \prod_{p=4k+1\le cN\log N}p^{v_p(P)}. $$  (Here,  $p$  always denotes a prime number.)

Since  $n^2+1$  is either odd or  $\equiv 2\pmod 4$ , we have  $v_2(P)\le \frac{N+1}2$ .

If  $p=4k+1$  is a prime, then the congruence  $x^2\equiv -1\pmod{p^\ell}$  has at most  $2$  solutions, because one can verify that  $p^\ell\mid x^2-y^2$  implies  $p^\ell\mid x\pm y$  if  $x,y$  are coprime to  $p$ . (Actually, one can show by induction that there are in fact exactly  $2$  solutions.) These solutions are of the form  $r$  and  $p^\ell-r$ , where  $0<r<\frac{p^\ell}2<(p^\ell-r)$ . Thus, every interval of the form  $[ap^\ell/2,(a+1)p^\ell/2)$  contains exactly one  $n$  satisfying  $p^\ell\mid n^2+1$ , proving us that  $p^\ell$  divides at most  $\frac{N}{p^\ell/2}+1$  factors of  $P(N)$ .

Furthermore, note that  $p^\ell$  divides none of the factors of  $P$  if  $p^\ell>N^2+1$ , i.e.  $\ell>\frac{\log(N^2+1)}{\log p}$ . Specifically, if  $p^2$  divides one of the factors of  $P$ , then  $p^2\le N^2+1<(N+1)^2$ , so  $p\le N$ .

So, proceeding as in the proof of Legendre's formula, we may write for  $p\le N$ ,  $$ v_p(P(N))\le \sum_{\ell=1}^{\lfloor \frac{\log(N^2+1)}{\log p}\rfloor }\left(\frac{N}{p^\ell/2}+1\right)= $$    $$ =\frac{\log(N^2+1)}{\log p}+2N\cdot \sum_{ \ell=1}^{\frac{\log(N^2+1)}{\log p}}\frac1{p^\ell}\le $$    $$ \le \frac{\log(N^2+1)}{\log p}+\frac{2N}{p-1}, $$  where the last estimate is true because  $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}p^{-k}=(p-1)^{-1}$ .

Further, if  $N<p<cN\log N$ , we simply have  $v_p(P(N))\le 2$ , because  $p^2$  divides none of  $1^2+1,\dots,N^2+1$ , and  $p$  divides exactly two of them.

Therefore, we have  $$ \log P=v_2(P)\log 2+\sum_{p=4k+1\le cN\log N}v_p(P)\log p\le  $$    $$ \le \frac{N+1}2\log 2+\sum_{p=4k+1\le N} \left(\frac{\log(N^2+1)}{\log p}+\frac{2N}{p-1}\right)\log p+\sum_{N<p=4k+1\le cN\log N}2\log p\le  $$  (now we use  $\sum_{p\le x}1=O(\frac{x}{\log x})$ ,  $\sum_{p\le x}\log p<x\log 4$  and that  $\sum_{p=4k+1\le x}\frac {\log p}{p-1}=\frac12\log x+O(1)$ :)  $$ \le O(N)+O(\frac{N}{\log N}\cdot \log (N^2+1))+2N\cdot \frac12\log N+2cN\log N\log 4 $$  On the other hand, using  $(N/e)^N<N!$ , we get  $(N/e)^{2N}<P(N)$ , so  $2N(\log N-1)<\log P$ .

The two combined give a contradiction for large enough  $N$  and  $c<\frac{1}{2\log 4}$ .**Note:**all the "high-powered results" we used here allow for an <details><summary>elementary proof</summary>The proof for  $\sum_{p\le x} \log p<x\log 4$  can be found [here](https://www.expii.com/t/elementary-proof-of-bertrands-postulate-7919). The same proof in fact shows more: that  $\text{lcm}(1,2,\dots,n)<4^n$ . Now, by observing the prime factorization, we have  $\text{lcm}(1,2,\dots,n)>\sqrt{n}^{\pi(n)}$ , where  $\pi(x)=\sum_{p\le x} 1$  - taking logarithms, we immediately get  $\pi(x)=O(\frac x{\log x})$ . Finally, note that  $\sum_{p=4k+1\le x}\frac {\log p}{p-1}=\frac12\log x+O(1)$  because one can easily show from  $\sum_{n\le x}n^{-t}=O(1)$  for  $t>1$  that  $\sum_{p=4k+1\le x}\frac {\log p}{p-1}-\sum_{p=4k+1\le x}\frac{\log p}{p}=O(1)$ . Now, to prove  $\sum_{p=4k+1\le x}\frac{\log p}{p}=\frac12\log x+O(1)$ , one needs to get much trickier.

Note that the simpler analogue of this, which is  $\sum_{p\le x}\frac{\log p}{p}=\log x+O(1)$ , comes from analyzing the prime factorization of  $\lfloor x\rfloor !$  - one can see from Legendre's formula that the exponent of some prime in this amount is close to  $x/p$ , and the logarithm of  $\prod p^{x/p}$  is  $x\sum \frac{\log p}{p}$ : hence the motivation (we need good upper and lower bounds to make this rigorous).

Although one can use elementary versions of the proof of [Dirichlet's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_character) to derive it, the handout containing the proof above was actually centered around proving  $\sum_{p=4k+1\le x}\frac{\log p}{p}=\frac12\log x+O(1)$  using Gaussian integers. It's actually an extension of our previous proof: it looks at  $\prod_{1\le |z|\le x} z$ , where  $z$  runs over Gaussian integers. We claim that for any  $p\equiv 1\pmod{4}$  greater than  $20$ , there is an  $n<\frac{1+2p-\sqrt{1+4p}}{4}$  such that  $p\mid n^2+1$ . Note this solves the problem, as the inequality rearranges to  $p>2n+\sqrt{2n}$ . 

First note we can choose an  $n\le \frac{p-1}{2}$ , as there two solutions to  $n^2+1\equiv 0\pmod{p}$ ; if  $n\equiv x$  is one of them, then  $p-x$  is the other, and one of these two is  $\le\frac{p-1}{2}$ . Thus let  $n=\frac{p-1}{2}-a$ . Note that  $n^2\equiv 1/4+a+a^2\equiv -1\pmod{p}$ , so  $p\mid (2a+1)^2+4$ . Thus,  $(2a+1)^2+4\ge p$ , or  $2a+1\ge \sqrt{p-4}$ . Thus,  $n\le \frac{p-1}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{p-4}-1}{2}=\frac{p-\sqrt{p-4}}{2}$ . Thus, it suffices to show  $\frac{p-\sqrt{p-4}}{2}<\frac{1+2p-\sqrt{1+4p}}{4}$ . This is equivalent to  $\sqrt{1+4p}<1+2\sqrt{p-4}$  which holds for  $p>20$ . Thus, the problem is solved.  $\square$

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$  be a prime (of which there are infinitely many), and let  $n$  be the smallest positive integer with  $p \mid n^2 + 1$ . Clearly  $0 \le n < p$ , and in fact,  $n < \frac{p}{2}$  (otherwise, take  $n \to p - n$ ).

Now, suppose that  $k$  is the smallest (odd) integer with  $p \mid \left(\frac{p - k}{2}\right)^2 + 1$ . We have  $p \mid (p - k)^2 + 4$ , or  $p \mid k^2 + 4$ , so  $k \ge \sqrt{p - 4}$ . Since  $n = \frac{p - k}{2}$ , we have
\[n = \frac{p - k}{2} \le \frac{p - \sqrt{p - 4}}{2},\]
so  $\sqrt{p - 4} \le p - 2n$ , or  $p - 4 \le (p - 2n)^2$ . This becomes  $p^2 - (4n + 1)p + 4(n^2 + 1) \ge 0$ . For the left hand side to be nonnegative, we must have  $p$  equal to or larger than the larger root of  $x^2 - (4n + 1)x + 4(n^2 + 1) = 0$ , or
\[p \ge \frac{(4n + 1) + \sqrt{(4n + 1)^2 - 16(n^2 + 1)}}{2} = \frac{4n + 1 + \sqrt{8n - 15}}{2} \ge 2n + \frac{1}{2} + \sqrt{2n - 4},\]
which is larger than  $2n + \sqrt{2n}$  for  $n$  large enough. We are done. (If our  $n$  is too small, pick a larger  $p$ ; the small  $n$  will only consume finitely many  $p$ .)</details>

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let us restate the problem as showing that there are infinitely many primes  $p$  such that there exists some positive integer  $n$  with  $n^2\equiv -1\pmod{p}$  and  $p>2n+\sqrt{2n}$ .

We know that  $-1$  is a square mod  $p$  if  $p\equiv 1\pmod{4}$ , and we know that there are infinitely many primes  $p\equiv 1\pmod{4}$ . Now, there is some  $n$  such that  $n^2\equiv -1\pmod{p}$ . However, if  $n^2\equiv -1\pmod{p}$ , then we also have  $(n-p)^2\equiv -1\pmod{p}$ . Therefore, we can pick such an  $n$  that is less than  $p/2$ . We are almost done, since we have now found such an  $n$  with  $p>2n$ . We just now need to get the  $\sqrt{2n}$ .

We will show that we can't have  $n$  be too close to  $p/2$ . Say  $n=(p-k)/2$  where  $k$  is odd. Then, say we had  $n^2\equiv -1\pmod{p}$ , so
\[4^{-1}(p^2-2pk+k^2)\equiv -1\pmod{p}\]or
\[k^2\equiv p-4\pmod{p}.\]If we choose  $k<\sqrt{p-4}$ , we can make sure this doesn't happen. Thus, any solution  $n$  must be less than  $(p-\sqrt{p-4})/2$ . Stated again, we can pick some  $n<(p-\sqrt{p-4})/2$  such that  $p\mid n^2+1$ . We will show this is enough to finish the problem. Note that
\begin{align*}
2n<p-\sqrt{p-4}&\implies\sqrt{p-4}<p-2n 
&\implies p-4 < p^2-4np+4n^2 
&\implies p^2 - (4n+1)p + 4(n^2+1) > 0 
&\implies p > \frac{(4n+1)+\sqrt{(4n+1)^2-16(n^2+1)}}{2}\text{ or } p<\frac{(4n+1)-\sqrt{(4n+1)^2-16(n^2+1)}}{2} 
&\implies p>\frac{(4n+1)+\sqrt{8n-15}}{2}\text { or }p<\frac{(4n+1)+\sqrt{8n-15}}{2}.
\end{align*}However, the second possibility violates  $2n<p-\sqrt{p-4}$ , so we must have that
\[p>\frac{(4n+1)+\sqrt{8n-15}}{2}=2n+1/2+\sqrt{2n-15/4}\]which for large enough  $p$  and  $n$  imply that
\[p>2n+\sqrt{2n}.\]Thus, we have shown that we can always pick  $p$  and  $n$  arbitrarily large so that  $p>2n+\sqrt{2n}$  and  $p\mid n^2+1$ .</details>

First, just looking at the problem, we understand that any such prime factor  $p$  must be  $1 \equiv \pmod{4}$  as  $4 \mid p-1$ . Clearly, we aren't going to get anywhere by starting off trying to find factors of  $n^2+1$ , a seemingly arbitrary number, so we might as well begin our search with a prime  $p$  and then try to find some  $n$  that works for  $p$ .

Hence, first we first rearrange the required condition to: $p>2n+\sqrt{2n} =>p-2n>\sqrt{2n} =>p^2+4n^2-4pn>2n=>4n^2-n(4p+2)+p^2>0$ .
Solving for roots,  $n=\frac{(4p+2) +- \sqrt{16p^2+4+16p-16p^2}}{8}=\frac{p}2 + \frac 14 +- \sqrt{ \frac p4 +\frac 1{16}}$ . $p-2n>0 => n< \frac{p}2 + \frac 14 - \sqrt{ \frac p4 +\frac 1{16}}$ .

I first came up with at least putting a bound on  $n$  while playing with primitive roots- basically, letting  $r$  be a primitive root,  $p$  must divide  $(r^2+1)(r^4+1)(r^6+1)....(r^{p-1}+1)$  if  $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ , as there exists some  $r^{\alpha} \equiv -1 \pmod{4}$ , and  $\alpha$  must be even when  $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$  (as then  $\alpha= \frac{p-1}2 =>r^{\alpha}=((r^{\frac{p-1}4})^2$ ). SolutionLet $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ be a prime (of which there are infinitely many), and let $n$ be the smallest positive integer with $p \mid n^2 + 1$ . Clearly $0 \le n < p$ , and in fact, $n < \frac{p}{2}$ (otherwise, take $n \to p - n$ ). Now, suppose that $k$ is the smallest (odd) integer with $p \mid \left(\frac{p - k}{2}\right)^2 + 1$ . We have $p \mid (p - k)^2 + 4$ , or $p \mid k^2 + 4$ , so $k \ge \sqrt{p - 4}$ . Since $n = \frac{p - k}{2}$ , we have \[n = \frac{p - k}{2} \le \frac{p - \sqrt{p - 4}}{2},\] so $\sqrt{p - 4} \le p - 2n$ , or $p - 4 \le (p - 2n)^2$ . This becomes $p^2 - (4n + 1)p + 4(n^2 + 1) \ge 0$ . For the left hand side to be nonnegative, we must have $p$ equal to or larger than the larger root of $x^2 - (4n + 1)x + 4(n^2 + 1) = 0$ , or \[p \ge \frac{(4n + 1) + \sqrt{(4n + 1)^2 - 16(n^2 + 1)}}{2} = \frac{4n + 1 + \sqrt{8n - 15}}{2} \ge 2n + \frac{1}{2} + \sqrt{2n - 4},\] which is larger than $2n + \sqrt{2n}$ for $n$ large enough. We are done. (If our $n$ is too small, pick a larger $p$ ; the small $n$ will only consume finitely many $p$ .)

solution_md: Comment $ \boxed{x \plus{} y \plus{} z \equal{} \frac {1}{x} \plus{} \frac {1}{y} \plus{} \frac {1}{z} \equal{} 1\Longrightarrow (x \minus{} 1)(y \minus{} 1)(z \minus{} 1) \equal{} 0}\ (xyz\neq 0)$ Here is my solution. Solution 1 By $ xyz \equal{} 1$ , we have $ \frac {x}{x \minus{} 1} \plus{} \frac {y}{y \minus{} 1} \plus{} \frac {z}{z \minus{} 1} \minus{} \left\{\frac {xy}{(x \minus{} 1)(y \minus{} 1)} \plus{} \frac {yz}{(y \minus{} 1)(z \minus{} 1)} \plus{} \frac {zx}{(z \minus{} 1)(x \minus{} 1)}\right\}$ $ \equal{} \frac {x(y \minus{} 1)(z \minus{} 1) \plus{} y(z \minus{} 1)(x \minus{} 1) \plus{} z(x \minus{} 1)(y \minus{} 1) \minus{} xy(z \minus{} 1) \minus{} yz(x \minus{} 1) \minus{} zx(y \minus{} 1)}{(x \minus{} 1)(y \minus{} 1)(z \minus{} 1)}$ $ \equal{} \frac {x(y \minus{} 1)(z \minus{} 1 \minus{} z) \plus{} y(z \minus{} 1)(x \minus{} 1 \minus{} x) \plus{} zx(y \minus{} 1 \minus{} y)}{(x \minus{} 1)(y \minus{} 1)(z \minus{} 1)}$ $ \equal{} \frac {x \plus{} y \plus{} z \minus{} (xy \plus{} yz \plus{} zx)}{(x \minus{} 1)(y \minus{} 1)(z \minus{} 1)}$ $ \equal{} \frac {x \plus{} y \plus{} z \minus{} (xy \plus{} yz \plus{} zx) \plus{} xyz \minus{} 1}{(x \minus{} 1)(y \minus{} 1)(z \minus{} 1)}$ $ \equal{} \frac {(x \minus{} 1)(y \minus{} 1)(z \minus{} 1)}{(x \minus{} 1)(y \minus{} 1)(z \minus{} 1)} \equal{} 1\ \because x\neq 1,\ y\neq 1,\ z\neq 1$ . $ \therefore \frac {x^2}{(x \minus{} 1)^2} \plus{} \frac {y^2}{(y \minus{} 1)^2} \plus{} \frac {z^2}{(z \minus{} 1)^2}$ $ \equal{} \left(\frac {x}{x \minus{} 1} \plus{} \frac {y}{y \minus{} 1} \plus{} \frac {z}{z \minus{} 1}\right)^2 \minus{} 2\left\{\frac {xy}{(x \minus{} 1)(y \minus{} 1)} \plus{} \frac {yz}{(y \minus{} 1)(z \minus{} 1)} \plus{} \frac {zx}{(z \minus{} 1)(x \minus{} 1)}\right\}$ $ \equal{} \left(\frac {x}{x \minus{} 1} \plus{} \frac {y}{y \minus{} 1} \plus{} \frac {z}{z \minus{} 1}\right)^2 \minus{} 2\left(\frac {x}{x \minus{} 1} \plus{} \frac {y}{y \minus{} 1} \plus{} \frac {z}{z \minus{} 1} \minus{} 1\right)$ $ \equal{} \left(\frac {x}{x \minus{} 1} \plus{} \frac {y}{y \minus{} 1} \plus{} \frac {z}{z \minus{} 1} \minus{} 1\right)^2 \plus{} 1\geq 1$ . The equality holds when $ \boxed{\frac {x}{x \minus{} 1} \plus{} \frac {y}{y \minus{} 1} \plus{} \frac {z}{z \minus{} 1} \equal{} 1 \Longleftrightarrow \frac {1}{x} \plus{} \frac {1}{y} \plus{} \frac {1}{z} \equal{} 3}$ . Solution 2 (a) Let $ x \plus{} y \plus{} z \equal{} a,\ xy \plus{} yz \plus{} zx \equal{} b,\ xyz \equal{} 1$ , $ x,\ y,\ z$ are the roots of the cubic equation : $ t^3 \minus{} at^2 \plus{} bt \minus{} 1 \equal{} 0$ . If $ t \equal{} 1$ is the roots of the equation, then we have $ 1^3 \minus{} a\cdot 1^2 \plus{} b\cdot 1 \minus{} 1 \equal{} 0\Longleftrightarrow a \minus{} b \equal{} 0\ \therefore t\neq 1\Longleftrightarrow a \minus{} b\neq 0$ . Thus the cubic equation with the roots $ \alpha \equal{} \frac {x}{x \minus{} 1},\ \beta \equal{} \frac {y}{y \minus{} 1},\ \gamma \equal{} \frac {z}{z \minus{} 1}$ is $ \left(\frac {t}{t \minus{} 1}\right)^3 \minus{} a\left(\frac {t}{t \minus{} 1}\right) \plus{} b\cdot \frac {t}{t \minus{} 1} \minus{} 1 \equal{} 0$ . $ \Longleftrightarrow (a \minus{} b)t^3 \minus{} (a \minus{} 2b \plus{} 3)t^2 \minus{} (b \minus{} 3)t \minus{} 1 \equal{} 0\ \cdots [*]$ . Let $ a \minus{} b \equal{} p\neq 0,\ b \minus{} 3 \equal{} q$ , we can rerwite the equation as $ pt^3 \minus{} (p \minus{} q)t^2 \minus{} qt \minus{} 1 \equal{} 0$ . By Vieta's formula, we have $ \alpha \plus{} \beta \plus{} \gamma \equal{} \frac {p \minus{} q}{p} \equal{} 1 \minus{} \frac {q}{p},\ \alpha \beta \plus{} \beta \gamma \plus{} \gamma \alpha \equal{} \minus{} \frac {q}{p}$ . $ \therefore \frac {x^2}{(x \minus{} 1)^2} \plus{} \frac {y^2}{(y \minus{} 1)^2} \plus{} \frac {z^2}{(z \minus{} 1)^2} \equal{} \alpha ^2 \plus{} \beta ^2 \plus{} \gamma ^2$ $ \equal{} (\alpha \plus{} \beta \plus{} \gamma)^2 \minus{} 2(\alpha \beta \plus{} \beta \gamma \plus{} \gamma \alpha)$ $ \equal{} \left(1 \minus{} \frac {q}{p}\right)^2 \minus{} 2\left( \minus{} \frac {q}{p}\right)$ $ \equal{} \left(\frac {q}{p}\right)^2 \plus{} 1\geq 1$ , the equality holds when $ \frac {q}{p} \equal{} 0\Longleftrightarrow q \equal{} 0\Longleftrightarrow b \equal{} 3$ , which completes the proof. If we clear denominators, we have
  \begin{align*}
    \sum_{cyc} x^2(y-1)^2(z - 1)^2 &\ge (x-1)^2(y-1)^2(z-1)^2 
    \sum_{cyc} x^2(yz - y - z + 1)^2 &\ge (x-1)^2(y-1)^2(z-1)^2 
    \sum_{cyc} x^2(y^2z^2 + y^2 + z^2 + 1 - 2y^2z - 2yz^2 + 4yz   - 2y - 2z) &\ge (x-1)^2(y-1)^2(z-1)^2 
    \sum_{cyc} 1 + 2x^2y^2 + x^2 - 4xy + 4x - 2x^2y - 2x^2z &\ge (x-1)^2(y-1)^2(z-1)^2 
  \end{align*}

  We then expand the right hand side
  \begin{align*}
    (x-1)^2(y-1)^2(z-1)^2 &= (xyz - xy - yz - xz + x + y + z - 1)^2 
    &= (x + y + z - xy - yz - zx)^2 
    &= (x + y + z)^2 + (xy + yz + zx)^2 - 2(x + y + z)(xy + yz + zx) 
    &= \sum_{cyc} x^2 + 2xy + \sum_{cyc} x^2y^2 + 2y - 2\sum_{cyc} (x^2y  + 1 + x^2z)
  \end{align*}

  We then will get some cancellation and end up with
  \begin{align*}
    \sum_{cyc} 3 + x^2y^2 - 6xy + 2x &\ge 0 
    \sum_{cyc} 3 + \frac{1}{z^2}  - \frac{6}{z} + \frac{2}{xy} &\ge 0 
    \left(\frac1x + \frac1y + \frac1z - 3\right)^2 &\ge 0
  \end{align*}

  This solves part (a). To find the equality cases, we see that we must have both  $\frac1x + \frac1y + \frac1z = 3$  and  $xyz = 1$ .

For convenience, let
   $(u, v, w) = \left(\frac1x, \frac1y, \frac1z\right)$ . Then, we want to solve
    $$ u + v + \frac{1}{uv} = 3. $$    Solving for  $u$  gives us
    $$ u = \frac{-v + 3 \pm (v-1)\sqrt{1 - \frac{4}{v}}}{2} $$    We therefore just require  $1 - \frac{4}{v}$  be a rational square, which is achievable for infinitely many rational  $v$ .

$(a)$   $\frac {x^{2}}{\left(x - 1\right)^{2}} + \frac {y^{2}}{\left(y - 1\right)^{2}} + \frac {z^{2}}{\left(z - 1\right)^{2}} = \sum_{cyc} \frac{1}{(1-yz)^2}$ Now let  $x=\frac{a}{b};y=\frac{b}{c};z=\frac{c}{a}$ . Now we have to prove that  $\sum_{cyc} \frac{1}{\left(1-\frac{b}{c}\cdot \frac{c}{a}\right)} \ge 1$ . Which is equivalent to  $\frac{(a^2b+b^2c+c^2a-3abc)^2}{(a-b)^2\cdot (b-c)^2\cdot (c-a)^2}\ge 0$ . Which is true.

For part  $(b)$  from last inequality we have that equality holds if  $a^2b+b^2c+c^2a-3abc=0$ . Dividing sides by  $abc$  we have  $\frac{a}{c}+\frac{b}{a}+\frac{c}{b}-3=\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{z}-3=\frac{xy+yz+zx}{xyz}-3=0 \Longleftrightarrow xy+yz+zx-3=xy+\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}-3=0$ . Multiplying sides by  $xy$  we get quadratic equation  $x^2y^2-3xy+x+y=x^2y^2-y(3x-1)+x=0$ . So  $y_{1,2}=\frac{1-3x\pm \sqrt{(3x-1)^2-4x^3}}{2x^2}$ . So  $y$  is rational iff discriminant  $(3x-1)^2-4x^3=(x-1)^2(1-4x)$  is a square.  $\Longleftrightarrow 1-4x=q^2$  i.e.  $x=\frac{1-q^2}{4}$ . So from here because  $x$  and  $y$  are rational from  $z=\frac{1}{xy}$  must be rational too.  $\blacksquare$

Then, replace  $x+y+z$  with  $x^2yz+xy^2z+xyz^2$ , so then you can make the substitution  $yz=a$ ,  $zx=b$ ,  $xy=c$ . It remains to prove that  $(a+b+c-3)^2 \ge 0$ , so you are finished with (a). There are better solutions to read for (a) than this one, so I condensed it.

For (b), I'll give the intuition. You first think in your head that  $2^2+3^2+6^2=7^2$ , and  $3^2+4^2+12^2=13^2$ . After you verify that  $4^2+5^2+20^2=21^2$ , you prove that  $m^2+(m+1)^2+(m^2+m)^2=(m^2+m+1)^2$  for all real numbers  $m$ . Then, you find  $x, y, z$  such that you can get   $$ (\frac{m}{m^2+m+1})^2+(\frac{m+1}{m^2+m+1})^2+(\frac{m^2+m}{m^2+m+1})^2=1 $$  For each of the fractions, there are two possible values for each of  $x$ ,  $y$ ,  $z$ .  $x$ ,  $y$ ,  $z$  all being positive does not lead to equality in the inequality, so you want two negative values. It is then natural to want to keep the value corresponding to  $\frac{m}{m^2+m+1}$  positive, while choosing the negative values for the other two. If this isn't natural, you can always just check the  $(2,3,6,7)$  case to see that the other two don't work. You find that in this scenario,  $xyz=1$ , so we satisfy the restrictive condition and equality. For part (a), let  $(a,b,c) = (\tfrac{x}{1-x},\tfrac{y}{1-y},\tfrac{z}{1-z}).$  Then given  $abc = (a+1)(b+1)(c+1)$ , or  $ab+bc+ca+a+b+c+1=0$ , we wish to show  $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 \geq 1$ . But
\begin{align*}
0 &\geq (a+b+c+1)^2 
&= (a^2+b^2+c^2) + 2(ab+bc+ca+a+b+c) + 1 
&= (a^2+b^2+c^2) + 2(-1) +1
&= (a^2+b^2+c^2)-1
\end{align*}
as desired.

For part (b), we equivalently wish to find infinitely many triples of rationals  $(a,b,c)$  such that  $$ a+b+c=-1 \quad \text{and} \quad ab+bc+ca=0. $$  So by Vieta's,  $b$  and  $c$  are roots of the quadratic  $x^2 + (a+1)x + a(a+1)$ . Thus, for  $b$  and  $c$  to be rational, its discriminant  $\Delta = (a+1)^2 - 4a(a+1) = -3a^2 - 2a + 1$  must be rational. But setting  $a = \tfrac{m}{n}$ , we wish for  $-3(\tfrac{m}{n})^2 - 2(\tfrac{m}{n})^2 + 1 = \tfrac{1}{n^2}(-3m^2 - 2mn+ n^2) = \tfrac{1}{n^2}((m-n)^2 - 4n^2)$  to be a square. But infinitely many  $(m,n)$  exist due to the infinitude of Pythagorean triples, as desired.

**(a)** Prove that \[\frac {x^{2}}{\left(x \minus{} 1\right)^{2}} \plus{} \frac {y^{2}}{\left(y \minus{} 1\right)^{2}} \plus{} \frac {z^{2}}{\left(z \minus{} 1\right)^{2}} \geq 1\] for all real numbers $x$ , $y$ , $z$ , each different from $1$ , and satisfying $xyz=1$ .
Let $\frac{x}{x-1}=\frac{a+1}{2a}$ , $\frac{y}{y-1}=\frac{b+1}{2b}$ , $\frac{z}{z-1}=\frac{c+1}{2c}$ , $a,b,c\ne0$ , then $a+b+c+abc=0$ and the inequality becomes $$ \frac2a+\frac2b+\frac2c+\frac1{a^2}+\frac1{b^2}+\frac1{c^2}\ge1, $$ $$ \left(\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c\right)^2+2\left(\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c\right)+1\ge0, $$ $$ \left(\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c+1\right)^2\ge0. $$

(a) Let  $a=\tfrac{x}{1-x}$  and define  $b,c$  similarly. Then  $x=\tfrac{a}{a+1}$ . So  $abc=(a+1)(b+1)(c+1)$ . Hence,  $(ab+bc+ca)+(a+b+c)=-1$ . Let  $m=ab+bc+ca,n=a+b+c$ . We know  $m+n=-1$ . We want to show  $a^2+b^2+c^2 = (a+b+c)^2-2(ab+bc+ca)\ge 1$ , i.e.  $n^2-2m\ge 1$ . But  $n=-1-m$ , so  $n^2-2m = (-1-m)^2-2m = 1+m^2 \ge 1$ . 

(b) Equality is achieved when  $m=0$ , and hence  $n=-1$ . So  $a+b+c=-1$  and  $ab+bc+ca=0$ . The latter gives  $c=-\tfrac{ab}{a+b}$ , and hence  $a+b-\tfrac{ab}{a+b}=-1$ , i.e.  $a^2+ab+b^2 = -a-b$ , i.e.  $a^2 + (b+1)a + b(b+1)=0$ . We want the discriminant of this quadratic in  $a$  to be the square of a rational:  $(b+1)^2 - 4b(b+1) = (b+1)(1-3b) = r^2$  for some  $r\in \mathbb{Q}$ . Let  $b=p/q$ . Then  $\tfrac{p+q}{q}\cdot \tfrac{q-3p}{q} = r^2$ , i.e.  $r^2=\tfrac{1}{q^2}(q+p)(q-3p)=\tfrac{1}{q^2}[(q-p)^2 - (2p)^2]$ . So  $(q-p)^2 - (2p)^2 = (qr)^2$ , i.e.  $(q-p)^2 = (2p)^2+(qr)^2$ . We can find infinitely many rational solution to Pythagoras, and hence we can find infinitely many rational  $r$  that work.

First, notice  $\frac{1}{az} = \frac{8k^3}{k^3 (k^2 + \sqrt{k^4 - 4k})^3} = (\frac{k^2 - \sqrt{k^4 - 4k}}{2k})^3$ . Then  $\frac{64k^6}{((k^2 - \sqrt{k^4 - 4k})^3 + 8k^3)^2}+ \frac{64k^6}{((k^2 + \sqrt{k^4 - 4k})^3 + 8k^3)^2}  + \frac{1}{(k^3 -1)^2} = \frac{64k^6 \cdot (128k^6 + 16k^3 (2k^6 + 6k^6 - 24k^3) + 2(4k^6 - 12k^3)^2 +  2(k^4 -4k) (4k^4 - 4k)^2) }{(64k^6 + 8k^3 (2k^6 + 6k^2 - 24k^3) + 64k^3)^2} + \frac{1}{(k^3 - 1)^2} = \frac{64k^3(2k^3 + 2k^6 - 6k^3) + (32k^{12} - 128k^9  + 288k^6) + (32k^{12} - 144k^9 + 288k^6 - 128k^3) }{64(k^3 - 1)^4} + \frac{1}{(k^3 - 1)^2} =\frac{64k^3 (k^3 - 1)^2 (k^3 - 2)}{(k^3 -1)^4} + \frac{1}{(k^3 - 1)^2} = 1$  as desired.

Then $ \left\|\begin{array}{cc} OA_1 \equal{} r_1^2 \plus{} OA'^2 OB_1 \equal{} r_2^2 \plus{} OB'^2 \end{array} \right\|$ . Let  $ M, N, and P$  be the midpoints of  $ AB$ ,  $ BC$ , and  $ CA$ , respectively.  Since  $ MNP$  is the medial triangle of  $ ABC$ , we use the resulting parallel lines to show  $ AH perpendicular MP, BH perpendicular MN, CH perpendicular PN$ .  Then,  $ AH$  is the radical axis of  $ rb$  and  $ rc$ ,  $ BH$  is the radical axis of  $ ra$  and  $ rc$ , and  $ CH$  is the radical axis of  $ ra$  and  $ rb$ .  Label  $ A1, A2, B1, B2, C1, C2$  such that going from B to C to A to B, you encounter them in that order. Let  $ O$  be the circumcenter of triangle  $ ABC$ .

Then, we have  $ (AC1)(AC2) \equal{} (AB2)(AB1)$ , using equal radii and the factorization of a difference of squares, this becomes $ (AC1)(AC2) \equal{} (AB2)(AB1)$  $ (AC1)(AC1 \plus{} 2 C1M) \equal{} (AB2)(AB2 \plus{} 2 B2P)$  $ ((AC1 \plus{} C1M) \minus{} C1M)((AC1 \plus{} C1M) \plus{} C1M) \equal{} ((AB2 \plus{} B2P) \minus{} B2P)((AB2 \plus{} B2P) \plus{} B2P)$  $ ((AC1 \plus{} C1M)^2 \minus{} (C1M)^2 \equal{} ((AB2 \plus{} B2P)^2 \minus{} (B2P)^2)$  $ (AM)^2 \minus{} (C1M)^2 \equal{} (AP)^2 \minus{} (B2P)^2$ 
Using Pythagoras on right triangles  $ OMC1$  and  $ OPB2$ , we have  $ (C1M)^2 \equal{} (OC1)^2 \minus{} (OM)^2$  and  $ (B2P)^2 \equal{} (OB2)^2 \minus{} (OP)^2$ 
so the equation becomes $ (AM)^2 \plus{} (OM)^2 \minus{} (OC1)^2 \equal{} (AP)^2 \plus{} (OP)^2 \minus{} (OB2)^2$ 
However,  $ (AM)^2 \plus{} (OM)^2 \equal{} (AP)^2 \plus{} (OP)^2 \equal{} (OA)^2 \equal{} (R)^2$  by the Pythagorean Theorem as well, where  $ R$  is triangle  $ ABC$ 's circumradius.  Hence,  $ OC1 \equal{} OB2$ , and repeating this for vertices  $ B$  and  $ C$  as well as noting that  $ O$ , the circumcenter, is the point of concurrency of the three perpendicular bisectors of triangle  $ ABC$  solves the problem.

We first show that quadrilateral  $B_1B_2C_1C_2$  is cyclic. This would imply that  $A$ , the intersection of  $B_1B_2$  and  $C_1C_2$  lies on the radical axis of the circles  $\Gamma_{B}$  and  $\Gamma_{C}$ . Thus, we would like to prove this. Let  $M$  be the midpoint of  $AB$ ,  $N$  be the midpoint of  $AC$ , and  $P$  be the midpoint of  $AB$ . Notice that the radical axis of two circles is perpendicular to the line through the centers of the circles. In this case, that line is  $NP$ . But since  $NP$  is the midline, it is parallel to  $BC$ . Thus, the radical axis is perpendicular to  $BC$ . However, since the two circles intersect at  $H$ , the radical axis also passes through  $H$ . Thus, it is the line  $AH$ , which implies that quadrilateral  $B_1B_2C_1C_2$  is cyclic.

Similarly, we can prove that quadrilaterals  $A_1A_2B_1B_2$  and  $A_1A_2C_1C_2$  are cyclic. The final step is to prove that the circumcircles of these three quadrilaterals are the same. We can proceed by two different methods.

Method 1: Since the center of a cyclic quadrilateral is the concurrency of the perpendicular bisectors of its sides, the center of  $B_1B_2C_1C_2$  is the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of  $B_1B_2$  and  $C_1C_2$ . However, these are also the perpendiculars to the sides  $AB$  and  $AC$  at the points  $P$  and  $N$ , respectively, which concur at  $O$ , the circumcenter of triangle  $ABC$ . Similarly, the centers of the other two cyclic quadrilaterals are also  $O$ , which means that they have the same center, which makes them the same circle. QED

Method 2: Proof by contradiction. Assume that the circles are different. The radical axes of the circles chosen pairwise are  $A_1A_2$ ,  $B_1B_2$ , and  $C_1C_2$ , which concur at the radical center. However, the radical axes are also the sides of triangle  $ABC$ , which do not concur. Thus, the assumption was not true and the circles are in fact the same. QED

In order for a statement to be true, the circumcenter must be exactly  $O$ , the center of the circumcircle of  $ABC$ . This motivates a following complex bash solution: Let  $ABC$  be the unit circle. The conditions on  $A_1$  are:
\[|a_1-m|=|h-m|\]
\[b+c=a_1+bc\overline{a_1}\]
Squaring and cross-multiplying we get:
\[(a_1-\frac{b+c}{2})(\overline{a_1}-\frac{b+c}{2bc})=\frac{2a+b+c}{2}\cdot \frac{2bc+ab+ac}{2abc}\]
Again:
\[RHS=a_1\overline{a_1}-\frac{b+c}{2bc}(b+c-bc\overline{a_1})-\frac{b+c}{2}\overline{a_1}+\frac{(b+c)^2}{4bc}=a_1\overline{a_1}-\frac{(b+c)^2}{4bc}\]
Finally, put constant on the other side to obtain:
\[|a_1|^2=\frac{(2a+b+c)(2bc+ab+ac)+a(b+c)^2}{4abc}=\frac{8abc+4\sum_{sym}a^2b}{4abc}\], that is symmetric wrt. to  $a,b,c$  and we are done (For other points analogous calculations do the trick).
Moral of the story: if a configuration is midpoint/orthocenter heavy, chances are that a complex bash will be clean (I did this one in about 10 minutes, if you have practiced bashing something of this kind would probably cross your mind at some moment)

Let  $ ABCD$  be a convex quadrilateral with  $ BA\neq BC$ . Denote the incircles of triangles  $ ABC$  and  $ ADC$  by  $ \omega_{1}$  and  $ \omega_{2}$  respectively. Suppose that there exists a circle  $ \omega$  tangent to ray  $ BA$  beyond  $ A$  and to the ray  $ BC$  beyond  $ C$ , which is also tangent to the lines  $ AD$  and  $ CD$ . Prove that the common external tangents to  $ \omega_{1}$  and  $\omega_{2}$  intersect on  $ \omega$ .


*Author: Vladimir Shmarov, Russia*
solution_md: So much pain and suffering.**Harmonic Solution:** First we define points. Let $\triangle AB C$ and $\triangle ACD$ have incenters $I_1$ and $I_2$ . Let $\overline{BA}$ , $\overline{CA}$ , $\overline{DA}$ and $\overline{DC}$ be tangent to $\omega$ at $E$ , $F$ , $G$ , and $H$ respectively. Let $O$ be the center of $(EFGH)$ , and define $Z = \overline{FH} \cap \overline{GE}$ . Let $X$ and $Y$ be the insimilicenter and exsimilicenter of $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ . Let $\overline{EF} \cap \overline{GH} = K$ . Finally let $P$ be the intersection of the tangents from $E$ and $H$ to $\omega$ . Similarly define $Q$ as the intersection of the tangents from $G$ and $F$ . Also define $N$ as the foot from $O$ to $\overline{AC}$ . Now note from La Hire's the polar of $K$ is $\overline{BD}$ . **Claim:** $K \in \overline{AC}$ . *Proof.* Complex bash with $(EFGH)$ as the unit circle. $\blacksquare$ **Claim:** $X \in \overline{BD}$ *Proof.* This follows from Monge d'Alembert on $\omega_1$ , $\omega_2$ and $\omega$ . $\blacksquare$ **Claim:** $X = \overline{EH} \cap \overline{FG}$ . *Proof.* Complex bash with $(EFGH)$ as the unit circle. Compute $X' = \overline{EH} \cap \overline{FG}$ and then show that it is collinear with $B$ and $D$ , and similarly with $A$ and $C$ . $\blacksquare$ Then from La Hire's $P$ lies on the polar of $X$ . Similarly $Q$ lies on the polar of $X$ , hence the polar of $X$ is exactly $\overline{PQ}$ .**Claim:** $K \in \overline{PQ}$ *Proof.* From La Hire's it suffices to show that $X$ lies on the polar of $K$ . However this is exactly $\overline{BD}$ so we are done. $\blacksquare$ **Claim:** $\overline{OZ} \perp \overline{AC}$ *Proof.* Observe that this follows from Brokards on complete quadrilateral $EFGH$ . We also find $Z \in \overline{BD}$ and $Z \in \overline{PQ}$ as a result of this Brokards application. $\blacksquare$ Now comes the tricky part, possibly incorrect. **Claim:** $\overline{OY} \perp \overline{AC}$ and hence $Y \in \overline{OZ}$ . *Proof.* Note we have that $(I_1I_1,XY) = -1$ . Then let $P_\infty$ denote the point at infinity along the line perpendicular to $\overline{AC}$ . Then projecting through $P_\infty$ to $\overline{AC}$ , $I_1$ and $I_2$ get sent to the incircle touch points of $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ say $S_1$ and $S_2$ , $X$ stays fixed and $Y$ maps to the foot from $Y$ to $\overline{AC}$ , say $N'$ . It suffices to show that $N' \equiv N$ , recalling that $N = \overline{OZ} \cap \overline{AC}$ . Then it suffices to show that $- 1 = (S_1S_2, XN)$ . Note $\frac{XS_1}{XS_2} = \frac{r_1}{r_2}$ where $r_1$ and $r_2$ denote the radii of $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ respectively. Then it suffices to show $\frac{NS_1}{NS_2} = \frac{r_1}{r_2}$ . However as $S_1$ and $S_2$ are symmetric about the midpoint of $\overline{AC}$ it suffices to show that $\frac{NC}{NA} = \frac{r_1}{r_2}$ . This is just a matter of computation (will edit in later). $\blacksquare$ Now assume for contradiction that $Y \not\in \omega$ . **Claim:** $Y$ coincides with $Z$ . *Proof.* Under inversion at $\omega$ we have $I_1 \mapsto I_1^*$ , $I_2 \mapsto I_2^*$ etc. Then note $I_1^* = \overline{OI_1} \cap \overline{EF}$ , $I_2^* = \overline{OI_2} \cap \overline{GH}$ and $X^* = \overline{OX} \cap \overline{PQ}$ . Also we have $\angle KI_1^*O =90$ . Similarly we also have $\angle KI_2^*O = 90$ and $\angle KX^*O = 90$ . However then $O$ , $I_1^*$ , $I_2^*$ , $X^*$ , $K$ and $N$ are all concyclic. Then obviously $Y$ is forced to map to $N = \overline{OZ} \cap (OI_1^*I_2^*X^*KN)$ as $I_1I_2XY$ is a line, and $Y$ cannot map to $O$ . $\blacksquare$ However then $Z$ , $I_1$ and $I_2$ must always be collinear. Now looking at the polars of $I_1$ and $I_2$ as well as the pole of $I_1I_2$ we can derive a contradiction. I will also add a more normal finish tomorrow + a more elementary solution.

**Lemma:** $ B,B'$  and  $ D'$  are collinear.

Clearly,  $ B$  and  $ D$  are the external and internal centers of similitude of  $ k;k_1$  and  $ k;k_2$  respectively. The Monge-d'Alembert circle theorem now says that  $ S$ , the intersection point of  $ AC$  and  $ BD$ , is the internal center of similitude of  $ k_1$  and  $ k_2$ .

\[ \frac{1}{h} = \frac{a-c}{\left| a-c \right|} \cdot i. \]
Now consider three homotheties: one centered at  $B$  sending  $k_1$  to  $k$  (in particular,  $c \mapsto \frac{2}{s+h}$ ), a negative homothety sending  $k$  to itself, and then the negative homothety at  $D$  sending  $k$  to  $k_2$  (in particular,  $\tfrac{2}{r+h} \mapsto c$ ).
That means their composition is
\[ z \mapsto \frac{c-d}{\frac{2}{r+h}-d} \left[ -\left( \frac{\frac{2}{s+h}-b}{c-b}(z-b)+b \right) -d \right] +d. \]
Now this composition sends  $k_1$  to  $k_2$  with positive ratio, so its center is the desired intersection point.  Now just compute the center (the homothety  $z \mapsto -Az + B$  has center  $B/(1+A)$ ), and then show that its magnitude is  $1$ .

Let  $K$  be the intersection of these tangents. Let  $I_1$ ,  $I_2$  and  $I$  be the centers of  $w_1$ ,  $w_2$  and  $w$ , respectively. We first require a lot of point definitions. Let  $\omega_1$  be tangent to  $\overline{AC}$  at  $P$ , and let  $Q$  be on  $\omega_1$  such that  $\overline{PQ}$  is a diameter. Similarly, let  $\omega_2$  be tangent to  $\overline{AC}$  at  $X$ , and let  $Y$  be on  $\omega_2$  such that  $\overline{XY}$  is a diameter. Let the line passing through the center of  $\omega$  perpendicular to  $\overline{AC}$  intersect the circle closer to  $\overline{AC}$  at  $T$ . 

We may check by lengths that (proof omitted since it requires quite a few point definitions)  $AB+AD = CB+CD$ . Now  $AP = 1/2(AC+AB-BC) = 1/2(AC+CD-AD) = CX$ . 

This implies that  $X$  is the  $A$ -excircle touchpoint of  $\triangle ABC$ , and  $P$  is the  $D$ -excircle touchpoint of  $\triangle ADC$ . Finally we may finish the proof. Note that as a result  $\overline{BQX}$  and  $\overline{DYP}$  are collinear. Moreover, as  $B$  is the exsimilicenter of  $\omega_1$  and  $\omega$ , and  $D$  is the insimilicenter of  $\omega_2$  and  $\omega$ , we have that  $\overline{BQT}$  and  $\overline{YDT}$  are collinear. Now  $\overline{QXT}$  and  $\overline{PYT}$  are collinear, so  $T$  is the exsimilicenter of  $\omega_1$  and  $\omega_2$ .

**Claim.** $AB + AD = CB + CD$ . *Proof.*
MotivationThe condition where there exists a circle $\omega$ tangent to the extension of four lines of the quadrilateral somehow reminds us of Pitot Theorem. Thus, we can try to form a similar claim.
Let $AB, BC, CD, DA$ tangent to $\omega$ at $X_1, X_4, X_2$ and $X_3$ respectively. Therefore, \[ AB + AD = (BX_1 - AX_1) + (AX_3 - DX_3) = BX_1 - DX_3 = BX_4 - DX_2 = (BX_4 - CX_4) + (CX_2 - DX_2) = CB + CD \] ------------- Now, let $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ tangent to $AC$ at $K$ and $J$ respectively. Notice that \[ AK = \frac{AB + AC - BC}{2} = \frac{CD + AC - AD}{2} = CJ \] Thus, $J$ is also the $B$ -excircle touch-point of $\triangle ABC$ with $AC$ .
NoteThis motivates us to draw $B$ -excircle wrt $\triangle ABC$ .
Now, by **Diameter of the Incircle** lemma, we know that if $K'$ and $J'$ are their antipode on respective incircles, then $(B,K', J)$ and $(D,J',K)$ are collinear. Now, we know that the exsimilicenter of $\omega_1, \omega_2$ concur with $K'J \equiv BJ, J'K \equiv DK$ as they are all "top" part of both circles $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ . Now, we just need to prove that $BJ \cap DK$ , which is the exsimilicenter of $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ lies on $\omega$ . Now, take point $L \in \omega$ such that the tangent of $\omega$ at $L$ is parallel to $AC$ . -----------**Claim.** $B,J,L$ collinear. *Proof.* To prove this, consider the homothety centered at point $B$ mapping the $B$ -excircle of $\triangle ABC$ to $\omega$ . This maps $J$ to $L$ by the way it is defined, and therefore, $B,J,L$ are collinear. --------**Claim.** $D,K,L$ collinear. *Proof.* To prove this consider the homothety centered at point $D$ mapping the $D$ -excircle of $\triangle ADC$ to $\omega$ . This maps $K$ to $L$ by the way it is defined, and therefore, $D,K,L$ are collinear. ------------- Hence, we know that $BJ \cap DK = L \in \omega$ by the way we define.

Let  $T_1$  and  $T_2$  be the touchpoints on  $\overline{AC}$ . The key claim is that  $\textbf{Claim:}$   $T_1$ ,  $T_2$  are extouch points as well.

Length chase. Note by Pitot that  $AB + AD = BC + CD$ . Letting  $W'$  be the tangency point of  $\omega_1$  with  $AB$ ,  $Y'$  the tangency point of  $\omega_2$  with  $AD$ , this yields the equation   $$ AT_1 + BW' + AT_2 + DY' = BW' + CT_1 + CT_2 + DY', $$   which becomes  $AT_1 + AT_2 = CT_1 + CT_2$  which implies  $AT_1 = CT_2$ , finishing the proof.

Now, homothety at  $P$  sends the bottommost point of  $\omega_2$  to  $T_1$ , and it sends  $T_2$  to the topmost point of  $\omega_1$ . However, by incircle lemma thingy from EGMO, the antipode of  $T_1$  lies on  $BT_2$  and similarly for  $\omega_2$ . 

At this point, a phantom point argument finishes. Let  $T_2'$  be the reflection of  $T_2$  over  $O_2$ , and let  $P'$  be the point closer to  $\overline{AC}$  satisfying  $\overline{OP} \perp \overline{AC}$ . Similarly define  $T_1'$ .

Homothety through  $D$  sends  $O_2$  to  $O$  and  $T_2'$  to  $P'$ , and homothety at  $B$  sends  $O_1$  to  $O$  and  $T_1'$  to  $P'$ . Thus  $P = P'$ , and we are done.

Let  $E = BA\cap D, F = BC\cap AD$ , and  $T_{1}, T_{2}$  the points where  $\omega_{1},\omega_{2}$  hit  $BC$ . Furthermore, let  $\omega$  be tangent to  $AB, BC, AD, DC$  at  $G, H, I, J$  respectively. Then, 
\[AB + AD = BG - AG + AI - DI = BH - DJ = BH - CH + CJ - DJ = BC + CD\]
Then, 
\[2*AT_{1} = AC + AB - BC = AC + CD - DC = CT_{2}\]

Thus,  $T_{1}$  is the extouch point of the D-excircle with  $AC$ . Let the  $D$  excircle be  $\Omega$ ; by Monges on  $\Omega, \omega_{1}, \omega_{2}$ , we have  $T_{1}, D,$  and the exsimile center of  $\omega_{1}, \omega_{2}$  collinear, so the exsimile center lies on  $T_{1}D$ . Similarly, it lies on  $BT_{2}$ , so it's on their intersection. We also know the exsimile center is the intersection of the common tangents to  $\omega_{1}, \omega_{2}$ , so now we need to prove  $DT_{1} \cap BT_{2}\in \omega$ .

Since  $D$  is the insimile center between  $\omega_{2}$  and  $\omega$  and  $DT_{2}$  intersects  $\omega_{2}$  at its southern point,  $T_{1}$  gets sent to the northern point of  $\omega$ . Similarly, since  $B$  the is eximile center of  $\omega$  and  $\omega_{1}$ , and  $BT_{2}$  intersects  $\omega_{1}$  at its northern point, it sends  $T_{2}$  to the northern point of  $\omega$ . We conclude that  $BT_{2}\cap DT_{1}$  lies on  $\omega$ , namely its northern point.

Let  $P$ , $Q$ , $R$ , $S$  the points where  $AB$ , $CD$ , $AD$ , $BC$  touch  $\omega$ . Also, let  $AC$  be tangent to  $\omega_1$ , $\omega_2$  at  $K$ , $L$ , respectively. Observe that   $$ AB+AD=BP-AP+AR-DR=BP-DR=BS-DQ=BS-CS+CQ-DQ=BC+CD \qquad (\spadesuit) $$  Furthermore,  $2AL= AC+AD-CD$ ,  $2CK= AC+BC-AB \implies$  from  $(\spadesuit)$ ,  $AD-CD=BC-AB \implies 2AL=2CK \implies AL=CK \implies L$  is the tangency point of the  $B$ -excircle of  $ABC$  with  $AC$ , call it  $\omega_B$ , and define  $\omega_D$  similarly.

Then,  $L$  is the excimilicenter of  $\omega_1$ , $\omega_B$ ,  $B$  is the excimilicenter of  $\omega_2$ , $\omega_B \implies$  by Monge's Theorem, the exmilicenter of  $\omega_1$ , $\omega_2$  lies on  $BL$ .

Similarly, the exmilicenter of  $\omega_1$ , $\omega_2$  lies on  $DK$  (applying Monge's Theorem WRT  $\omega_1$ , $\omega_2$ , $\omega_D$ ).

Hence, the exmilicenter of  $\omega_1$ ,  $\omega_2$  is  $BL \cap DK$ . 

Now, consider the positive homothety centered at  $B$  mapping  $\omega_B \mapsto \omega$ .

The image of  $L$  is a point  $X_B \in \omega$  such that the tangent through  $X_B$  to  $\omega$  is parallel to  $AC$ , since the tangent through  $L$  to  $\omega_B$  is  $AC$ , and  $X_B$  is the nearest point to  $AC$  which satisfies these conditions.  $(\star)$ Similarly, consider the negative homothety centered at  $D$  mapping  $\omega_D \mapsto \omega$ .

The image of  $K$  is a point  $X_D \in \omega$  such that the tangent through  $X_D$  to  $\omega$  is parallel to  $AC$ , since the tangent through  $K$  to  $\omega_D$  is  $AC$ , and  $X_B$  is the nearest point to  $AC$  which satisfies these conditions.  $(\star \star)$ From  $(\star)$  and  $(\star \star)$ , since the point  $X \in \omega$  such that the tangent through  $X$  to  $\omega$  is parallel to  $AC$  and nearest to  $AC$  is unique, we have that  $X_B=X_D \in \omega \implies BL \cap DK \in \omega$ , and since the exmilicenter of any two circle is, by definition, the intersection of the external common tangents to these circles, we are done. $\blacksquare$

nice problem. Let  $T_1, T_2$  be the tangency points of  $\omega_1$  and  $\omega_2$  to  $AC$  respectively. **Claim:**  $T_1,$   $T_2$  are extouch points of  $\triangle ADC$  and  $\triangle ABC$  respectively.
*Proof:* 

First define a bunch of points. Let  $P = AB \cap CD$  and  $Q = AD \cap BC.$  Let  $W, X, Y, Z$  be the tangency points of  $\omega$  to lines  $AB, CD, AD,$  and  $BC$  respectively. Then,  $X$  is the  $A$ -extouch point of  $APD$  and  $Y$  is the  $C$ -extouch point of  $CDQ,$  meaning \[ PX = PW = \frac{AD +PD - AP}{2}, \quad QY = QZ = \frac{QD +  DC - CQ}{2}. \] Let  $C'$  and  $A'$  be the  $A$  and  $C$  intouch points. Then, \[ C'W = A'Z \iff \frac{AB+AC-BC}{2} + \frac{AP+PD+AD}{2} = \frac{AC+BC-AB}{2} + \frac{QD+DC+CQ}{2}. \] Furthermore, nothing that  $DX = DY,$  \[ \frac{AP+PD-AD}{2} = \frac{CQ+DQ-CD}{2}. \] The above two lines combined quickly gives  $AD +AB = BC + DC,$  which in turn gives \[AT_1 = \frac{AB+AC-BC}{2} = CT_2 = \frac{AC+CD-AD}{2}. \] as desired.

Now, note that there is a homothety centered at  $T_2$  sending  $\omega_2$  to the excircle of  $BAC,$  which in turn can be mapped to  $\omega$  via homothety at  $B.$  Therefore, the center of homothety sending  $\omega_2$  to  $\omega$  must lie on line  $BT_2.$  Furthermore, since the intersection of tangents of  $\omega_1$  and  $\omega_2$  is the exsimilicenter of  $\omega_1$  and  $\omega_2,$  it must lie on the line connecting the centers of  $\omega_1$  and  $\omega_2,$  say  $I_1$  and  $I_2$  respectively. (alternatively, use Monge)**Claim:**  $I_1I_2,$   $BT_2,$  and  $DT_1$  are concurrent.
*Proof:*

It's well known that  $DT_1$  passes through the antipode of  $T_2$  with respect to  $\omega_1,$  say  $D',$  and similarly  $BT_2$  passes through the antipode of  $T_1,$  say  $B'.$  Then,  $I_1$  and  $I_2$  are the corresponding midpoints of  $T_1B'$  and  $T_2D',$  and now it's easy to see the concurrence since  $T_1B' \parallel T_2D'$  and we want to connect their midpoints.

Let the homothety at  $D$  send  $D'$  to  $K,$  where  $K$  is on  $\omega.$  Then, if  $K'$  is the antipode of  $K,$   $KK' \parallel D'T_2 \parallel B'T_1.$  However, this in turn implies that  $K$  lies on  $B'T_2,$  since a homothety at  $B$  maps  $B'$  to  $K$  due to the uniqueness of  $K.$  Hence,  $K = BT_2 \cap DT_1,$  which is the desired point that lies on  $\omega.$   $\blacksquare$

Then   $$ BA+AD+DL = BA + AL = BA +AE = BE = BF = BC + CF = BC + CK = BC + CD + DK $$   and consequently   $$ BA + AD = BC + CD $$  Moreover, let  $P$  and  $Q$  be the points of tangency of  $AC$  on with  $\omega_1, \omega_2$ . 
Then   $$ AP = \frac{1}{2} \cdot (AC+AB-BC) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot (AC + CD - DA) = CQ $$  Then if we let the antipodes of  $P$  and  $Q$  in  $\omega_1, \omega_2$  respsectively be  $P'$  and  $Q'$ , by Diameter of Incircle Lemma, if we let the tangency point of the tangent parallel to  $AC$  that is closer to  $AC$  to  $\omega$  be  $T$ , we have that  $B,P'Q,T$  and  $T, D, Q', P$  are collinear. 
Notice that as  $PP'$  and  $QQ'$  are diameters, the common external tangents of the two circles must intersect at  $T$  which by definition lies on  $\omega$ .  $\blacksquare$

Let  $ n$  and  $ k$  be positive integers with  $ k \geq n$  and  $ k \minus{} n$  an even number. Let  $ 2n$  lamps labelled  $ 1$ ,  $ 2$ , ...,  $ 2n$  be given, each of which can be either *on* or *off*. Initially all the lamps are off. We consider sequences of steps: at each step one of the lamps is switched (from on to off or from off to on).

Let  $ N$  be the number of such sequences consisting of  $ k$  steps and resulting in the state where lamps  $ 1$  through  $ n$  are all on, and lamps  $ n \plus{} 1$  through  $ 2n$  are all off.

Let  $ M$  be number of such sequences consisting of  $ k$  steps, resulting in the state where lamps  $ 1$  through  $ n$  are all on, and lamps  $ n \plus{} 1$  through  $ 2n$  are all off, but where none of the lamps  $ n \plus{} 1$  through  $ 2n$  is ever switched on.

Determine  $ \frac {N}{M}$ .


*Author: Bruno Le Floch and Ilia Smilga, France*

Let  $ S_N, S_M$  be the sets of sequences with the respective definitions given in the problem ( $ |S_N| \equal{} N, |S_M| \equal{} M$ ). We show a  $ 1$  to  $ 2^{k\minus{}n}$  correspondence from  $ S_M$  to  $ S_N$ .

Take an arbitrary sequence in  $ S_M$ . Only the numbers  $ 1$  through  $ n$  appear and each appears an odd number of times. Given a number  $ i$ ,  $ 1 \leq i \leq n$ , pick an even number of occurrences of that number in the sequence and replace them with  $ n\plus{}i$ . If  $ i$  appears  $ 2m_i\plus{}1$  times, there are
\[ {2m_i\plus{}1 \choose 0} \plus{} {2m_i\plus{}1 \choose 2} \plus{} \ldots \plus{} {2m_i\plus{}1 \choose 2m_i} \equal{} 2^{2m_i}\]
ways to do this. We can determine that  $ \sum m_i \equal{} \frac{\sum ( 2m_i \plus{} 1) \minus{} n}{2} \equal{} \frac{k\minus{}n}{2}$ . Then the total number of ways is  $ \prod 2^{2m_i} \equal{} 2^{2 \sum m_i} \equal{} \boxed{2^{k\minus{}n}}$ .

No sequence in  $ S_N$  is obtained twice in the way. Note that each element is invariant mod  $ n$  in the correspondence. So if two sequences in  $ S_M$  gave the same one in  $ S_N$ , they would be the same mod  $ n$  and thus the same sequence. All sequences in  $ S_N$  are also obtained; just take each element mod  $ n$  again (using residue classes  $ 1, 2, \ldots n$ ) and this gives a sequence in  $ S_M$  which generates the one you picked in  $ S_N$ .

By the Roots of Unity Filter, this means \[M = \frac{\sum_{(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in \{-1, 1\}^n} p(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}{2^n},\] since a term $\prod x_i^{e_i}$ contributes $2^n$ to the sum if all the $e_i$ are even (every contribution is $1$ , and there are $2^n$ tuples), and $0$ to the sum otherwise (if $e_i$ is odd, then toggling the sign of $x_i$ gives terms which cancel out). So then using our definition of $p$ , we have \[M = \frac{\sum_{(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in \{-1, 1\}^n} x_1\cdots x_n(x_1 + \cdots + x_n)^k}{2^n}.\] For each $0 \leq m \leq n$ , there are $\tbinom{n}{m}$ $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ with exactly $m$ terms which are $-1$ , and each such term contributes $(-1)^m(n - 2m)^k$ to the sum, so then \[M = \frac{1}{2^n} \sum_{m = 0}^n \binom{n}{m}(-1)^m(n - 2m)^k.\] Meanwhile, to find $N$ , consider the polynomial \[q(x_1, \ldots, x_{2n}) = x_1x_2\cdots x_n(x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_{2n})^k.\] Then $N$ is again the sum of the coefficients of the terms of $q$ with an even exponent ineach of the $x_i$ (because the expansion of $(x_1 + \cdots + x_{2n})^k$ contains a term for each possible sequence of $k$ switches, and a sequence counts iff it has an odd exponent of each of $x_1$ , \ldots, $x_n$ and an even exponent of $x_{n + 1}$ , \ldots, $x_{2n}$ ). By the same Roots of Unity Filter argument as before, this means \[N = \frac{\sum_{(x_1, \ldots, x_{2n}) \in \{-1, 1\}^{2n}} x_1\cdots x_n(x_1 + \cdots + x_{2n})^k}{2^{2n}}.\] Let $e(n, m)$ be the number of ways to choose $(x_1, \ldots, x_{2n}) \in \{-1, 1\}^{2n}$ such that $m$ of the $x_i$ are $-1$ and $x_1\ldots x_n = 1$ (equivalently, an even number of $x_1$ , \ldots, $x_n$ are $-1$ ), and $o(n, m)$ the number of ways such that $x_1\ldots x_n = -1$ (equivalently, an odd number of $x_1$ , \ldots, $x_n$ are $-1$ ). Then for each $0 \leq m \leq 2n$ , if $m$ of the $x_i$ are $-1$ , we get a contribution of \[(e(n, m) - o(n, m))\cdot (2n - 2m)^k\] (since there are $e(n, m)$ such terms with $x_1\cdots x_n = 1$ , and $o(n, m)$ with $x_1\cdots x_n = -1$ , and we always have $x_1 + \cdots + x_{2n} = 2n - 2m$ ). This means \[N = \frac{1}{2^{2n}} \sum_{m = 0}^{2n} (e(n, m) - o(n, m))(2n - 2m)^k.\] **Claim:** For any $0 \leq m \leq 2n$ , we have \[e(n, m) - o(n, m) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } m \text{ is odd}, (-1)^\ell\binom{n}{\ell} & \text{if } m = 2\ell.\end{cases}\] *Proof.* For each $0 \leq i \leq n$ , let $e_i(n, m)$ and $o_i(n, m)$ be the number of ways to choose $(x_1, \ldots, x_{2n})$ satisfying the given constraints, such that we also have $x_j = x_{n + j}$ for all $1 \leq j \leq i$ (so $e_0$ and $o_0$ are the same as $e$ and $o$ ). Then we claim that for each $0 \leq i < n$ , we have \[e_i(n, m) - o_i(n, m) = e_{i + 1}(n, m) - o_{i + 1}(n, m).\] This is because $e_i(n, m) - e_{i + 1}(n, m)$ counts the number of $(x_1, \ldots, x_{2n})$ satisfying the given constraints for $e$ with $x_j = x_{n + j}$ for all $1 \leq j \leq i$ and $x_{i + 1} \neq x_{n + i + 1}$ , and the same is true for $o_i(n, m) - o_{i + 1}(n, m)$ . But these counts must be equal, since for any sequence with $x_j = x_{n + j}$ for all $1 \leq j \leq i$ and $x_{i + 1} \neq x_{n + i + 1}$ , swapping $x_i$ and $x_{n + i + 1}$ toggles whether the sequence contributes to $e_i(n, m) - e_{i + 1}(n, m)$ or $o_i(n, m) - o_{i + 1}(n, m)$ . So then we have \[e(n, m) - o(n, m) = e_n(n, m) - o_n(n, m).\] If $m$ is odd then these are both $0$ , as we cannot have $(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = (x_{n + 1}, \ldots, x_{2n})$ (this would mean an even number of $-1$ 's). If $m = 2\ell$ , then there are $\binom{n}{\ell}$ solutions with $(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = (x_{n + 1}, \ldots, x_{2n})$ (choose any $\ell$ of the first $n$ to be $-1$ 's), and this contributes to $e_n$ if $\ell$ is even and $o_n$ if $\ell$ is odd. stem_md:
A deck of  $n > 1$  cards is given. A positive integer is written on each card. The deck has the property that the arithmetic mean of the numbers on each pair of cards is also the geometric mean of the numbers on some collection of one or more cards.
For which  $n$  does it follow that the numbers on the cards are all equal?

*Proposed by Oleg Košik, Estonia*

We will use the following $\color{red} \rule{2.5cm}{2pt}$  $\color{red} \clubsuit$   $\color{red} \boxed{\textbf{Lemma.}}$   $\color{red} \clubsuit$  $\color{red} \rule{2.5cm}{2pt}$ Let  $a$  and  $b$  be two natural numbers,  $b \ge a$ . Then, for  $c_1, c_2, \dots, c_n$  natural numbers such that  $a \ge c_1 \ge c_2 \ge ... \ge c_n$ , we have  $$ \frac{a+b}{2}\ge \sqrt[n+2]{a\cdot b \cdot c_1 \cdot c_2 \cdot ... \cdot c_n}. $$  Equality occurs IF and ONLY IF  $a=b=c_1=c_2=...=c_n$ .***Proof:***
Applying AM-GM, we get  $$ \frac{a+b}{2} \ge \sqrt{ab}. $$  We will now prove, by induction, that  $\sqrt{ab} \ge \sqrt[m]{a\cdot b\cdot c_1 \cdot ... \cdot c_{m-2} }$  for any  $m$ , provided that  $c_1 \ge c_2 \ge c_3 \ge ... \ge c_{m-2}$ . $\color{green} \rule{3.9cm}{2pt}$  $\color{green} \clubsuit$   $\color{green} \boxed{\textbf{Induction basis.}}$   $\color{green} \clubsuit$  $\color{green} \rule{3.9cm}{2pt}$   $$ \sqrt{ab}=a^{\frac{3}{6}}b^{\frac{3}{6}} $$    $$ \sqrt{abc_1}=a^{\frac{2}{6}}b^{\frac{2}{6}}c^{\frac{2}{6}} $$  Since all three numbers are natural, it suffices to verify that  $a^{\frac 16}b^{\frac 16} \ge c^{\frac 13}$ , which is true from  $b\ge a \ge c_1$ . Equality only occurs exactly when  $c_1^2=ab$ , which is equivalent to  $b=a=c_1$ . $\color{green} \rule{4.9cm}{2pt}$  $\color{green} \spadesuit$   $\color{green} \boxed{\textbf{Induction hypothesis.}}$   $\color{green} \spadesuit$  $\color{green} \rule{4.9cm}{2pt}$ Let us suppose that   $$ \sqrt{ab} \ge \sqrt[m]{a\cdot b\cdot c_1 \cdot ... \cdot c_{m-2} } $$  for some natural number  $m$ . $\color{green} \rule{3.9cm}{2pt}$  $\color{green} \bigstar$   $\color{green} \boxed{\textbf{Induction step.}}$   $\color{green} \bigstar$  $\color{green} \rule{3.9cm}{2pt}$ For  $m+1$ , we aim to prove that  $$ \sqrt{ab} \ge \sqrt[m+1]{a\cdot b\cdot c_1 \cdot ... \cdot c_{m-1} }. $$  Since the induction hypothesis has given us the evaluation that  $\sqrt{ab} \ge \sqrt[m]{a\cdot b\cdot c_1 \cdot ... \cdot c_{m-2} }$ , it suffices to show that   $$ \sqrt[m]{a\cdot b\cdot c_1 \cdot ... \cdot c_{m-2} } \ge \sqrt[m+1]{a\cdot b\cdot c_1 \cdot ... \cdot c_{m-1} }. $$  Raising to the  $m(m+1)$ =th power, we obtain  $$ a^{m+1}b^{m+1}c_1^{m+1}...c_{m-2}^{m+1} \ge a^m b^m c_1^m...c_{m-1}^m $$  which reduces to  $$ abc_1...c_{m-2} \ge c^m_{m-1}=\underbrace{c_{m-1}c_{m-1}...}_{m \text{ times}}. $$  Since every single multiplier of  $LHS$  is greater than or equal to every single one of  $RHS$ , we are done (equality occurs if and only if all numbers are equal).  $\color{red} \rule{4.8cm}{2pt}$  $\color{red} \spadesuit$   $\color{red} \boxed{\textbf{Applying the lemma.}}$   $\color{red} \spadesuit$  $\color{red} \rule{4.8cm}{2pt}$ Taking all cards of the deck, we sort them by how big the integer written on them is (if two numbers are equal, then in the sorting, they will just be next to each other, no big deal). Then, fixing  $b$  as the largest number and  $a$  as the second largest, and assuming that  $a \neq b$ , all inequalities shown are strict, so we get a contradiction - the arithmetic mean of  $a$  and  $b$  cannot be expressed as a geometric mean of some of the other numbers. This then implies that the two greatest numbers must be equal, so let  $d$  be the greatest number which is **NOT** equal to  $b$  now.
Since we are working with natural numbers, the number  $\frac{b+d}{2}$  has to have a divisor  $p$ , where  $p$  is a prime divisor of  $b$ . Then  $d$  also has  $p$  as its divisor, and, repeating this, we get that all members of our "sequence" have the same prime divisors. That means that we can divide all members by  $c_n$ .
<details><summary>*</summary>(If a deck of cards satisfies the problem condition, then by dividing all numbers on the cards by their greatest common divisor, we still obtain a deck that satisfies the problem condition)</details>
Finally,  $c_n=1$ , so taking the arithmetic mean of it and the second-smallest (non- $1$ ) number suffices, as this mean cannot possibly be derived from a geometric mean of other numbers due to them all having the same prime factors and due to it not having them as prime factors. The only condition where this is not true is when  $c_n=1=b$ , thus all numbers are equal.
Since this solution works considering arbitrary  $n$ , we conclude that all numbers on the cards are equal for all  $n$ .

Let the  $n$  numbers be  $a_1 \le a_2 \le \ldots \le a_n$ . Let  $d = \gcd (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n)$ . Suppose  $a_n \ne d$ . Divide  $d$  throughout to get  $b_1 \le b_2 \le \cdots \le b_n$  where the same property holds, except now the gcd is  $1$ , and  $b_n > 1$ . Let  $p$  be a prime factor of  $b_n$ . Let  $i$  be the largest index for which  $p \nmid b_i$ ; such an  $i$  exists as the gcd is  $1$ . Also note that  $i \le n-1$ .

Consider the number   $$  m = \frac{b_i + b_{i+1}}{2} $$    $p \nmid m$ , clearly. But  $m > b_i$ , so if  $m$  is a geometric mean of a non-empty subset of integers in  $\{b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n\}$ , then one of the integers used must be  $b_j$  for some  $j \ge i+1$ . But  $p \mid b_j$ , so  $p \mid m$ , which is a contradiction.

Therefore  $a_n = d$ , so  $a_1 = a_2 = \ldots = a_n = d$ .

We see that if some common prime $p$ divides all terms $a_1, a_2 \dots a_n$ , we divide that prime number $p$ from all numbers on the cards and every equality between the $\text{AM}$ and $\text{GM}$ would still hold so we divide all numbers by suitable exponents of suitable primes such that in the new sequence we have $\text{gcd}(a_1, a_2, a_3 \dots a_n) = 1$ and $a_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ for all $i \in \{ 1, 2, 3 \dots n \}$ . Let us say a prime $p$ divides the number $a_1$ . We use induction hypothesis to show that $p \lvert a_k$ for $k = \{ 1, 2, 3 \dots n \}$ . Let us say that for all $i \leq x$ prime $p$ divides $a_i$ . Then, if $a_{x+1} = a_x$ then $p \lvert a_{x+1}$ otherwise due to the conditions of the problem, $\text{AM}(a_{x+1}, a_x) = \dfrac{a_{x+1} + a_x}{2} \geq a_{x+1}$ and so if $\text{AM}(a_{x+1}, a_x) = \sqrt[r]{a_w \cdot a_y \cdot \dots a_z}$ where there are $r$ terms in the sequence $a_x, a_y, \dots a_z$ , then one of the numbers in the sequence must be greater than or equal to $a_x$ so that $\text{AM}(a_{x+1}) \geq a_{x+1}$ and due to the induction hypothesis, we see that $p \lvert a_{x+1}$ as desired. But this contradicts $\text{gcd}(a_1, a_2, a_3 \dots a_n) = 1$ , so $a_1 = 1$ in the new sequence and so $a_i = 1$ for $i = \{ 1, 2, 3 \dots n \}$ implying that all the numbers on the cards are equal for all positive integers $n$ .

The answer is all  $n$ .
First WLOG let the gcd of all of the integers be  $1$ , since otherwise we can just scale down and nothing changes. Realize that this implies all of the cards must be odd, since if there exists one odd and one even number, their arithmetic mean will be noninteger, but it must also equal an algebraic integer (impossible). Also let the cards be  $a_1\leq a_2 \leq \cdots \leq a_n$ .
Now, suppose a prime  $p$  divides  $a_n$ . We will show that  $p$  must divide  $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{n-1}$  as well by strong induction.
Our base case is obviously true because of our supposition. Now supose that for some  $k$ ,  $p$  divides  $a_{k+1},a_{k+2},\ldots,a_n$ . Now consider  $\frac{a_{k}+a_n}{2}$ . If  $a_k=a_n$  then  $p$  obviously divides  $a_k$ , so henceforth assume  $a_k<a_n$ . Then clearly the geometric mean which equals this fraction must contain some number  $a_i$  where  $i>k$ , otherwise it is at most  $a_k$  which is less than  $\frac{a_k+a_n}{2}$ . But since  $p$  divides this  $a_i$ , the geometric mean must be divisible by  $p$ . Now taking  $\pmod{p}$  and remembering that all the numbers are odd, we get:  $$ \frac{a_k+a_n}{2} \equiv 0 \pmod{p} \implies a_k \equiv 0 \pmod{p} $$  so  $p$  divides  $a_k$  as well, which completes the induction and shows that  $p \mid \gcd(a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n)$ . However the existence of such a  $p$  contradicts the fact that the gcd of all of the integers is  $1$ , so such a  $p$  cannot exist, which implies  $a_n=1$ . Since the cards are positive integers and  $a_n$  is the largest, it follows that all of the other cards are  $1$  as well, so they are equal as desired.
