SolutionLemma 1. There exists a line separating the points such that the distances from the points to the line is at least $D/2N$ .
ProofSuppose that $P,Q$ are two points such that the distance between them is $D$ . Let $\pi:\real^2\to \real$ be the orthogonal projection map projecting to the line $PQ$ . Then $N$ points divide $PQ$ into $N-1$ intervals, which shows that there exists an interval that has length at least $D/(N-1)$ . Then we can take the perpendicular bisector of the interval, and this satisfies the desired conditions.
Up to a constant, we can interpret the maximum value of $d$ among all the choices of line as follows: every (open) strip of width $d$ that has points on both sides (outside the strip) contain at least one point. We will use this interpretation in the proof. Lemma 2. There exists a positive absolute constant $c''$ such that \[\frac{1}{d^2}\leq c''D.\]
ProofWe can assume that $d$ is sufficiently small, for example $d=O(N^{-0.1})$ , for otherwise there is nothing to prove. Let $P$ be the boundary of the convex hull of the $N$ points. Let $S$ be the subset of $N$ points containing all the points whose distance from $P$ is at most $1/2$ . Then by the same argument in Lemma 1., to bound the number of points in $S$ it suffices to bound the area of the region of points with distance $\leq 1$ from $P$ . The perimeter of $P$ is at most, say, $4D$ . Since $D=\Omega(\sqrt{N})$ , $D$ is much larger than $1$ when $N$ is sufficiently large, which shows that the area is $\Theta(D)$ . Therefore $|S|\lesssim D$ . Now it suffices to show that $d^{-2}\lesssim |S|$ . Take an arbitrary line $L$ and orient it by identifying it with $\real$ . For any angle $\theta$ , let $L_{\theta}$ be the oriented line obtained by rotating $L$ by angle $\theta$ counterclockwise. Let $\pi_{\theta}$ be the orthogonal projection onto $L_{\theta}$ , and let $m_{\theta}$ be the minimum of the image of the $N$ points under $\pi_{\theta}$ . Let $S_{\theta}$ be the preimage of $[m_{\theta}, m_{\theta}+1/2]$ under $\pi_{\theta}$ . It is clear that $S_{\theta}\subseteq S$ . Moreover, by the definition of $d$ , we know that \[\pi_{\theta}^{-1}((m_{\theta}+(n-1)d, m_{\theta}+nd))\] is nonempty for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ . Hence $|S_{\theta}|\gtrsim d^{-1}$ . Therefore to show that $d^{-2}\lesssim |S|$ , we would like to show that $S_{\theta}$ 's cannot share too many elements. Let us focus on a certain $\theta$ for now. WLOG assume that $L_{\theta}$ is exactly the $x$ -axis. Then for any $(p,q),(r,s)\in S_{\theta}$ , we have $|p-r|\leq 1/2$ . Hence \[1\leq (p-r)^2+(q-s)^2 = (q-s)^2+\frac{1}{4},\] which shows that $|q-s|>1/2.$ Let $t = |S_{\theta}|$ for now,and let $(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_t,y_t)$ be the elements of $S_{\theta}$ such that $y_0\leq y_1\leq \cdots\leq y_{t-1}$ . Then from what we have shown, we know that for all $i\geq t/2$ , we have $y_i-y_0 > t/4\gtrsim d^{-1}$ . Therefore we have \[\pi_{\theta+\delta}((x_i,y_i))-\pi_{\theta+\delta}((x_0,y_0)) = (x_i-x_0)\cos\delta + (y_i-y_0)\sin\delta>\frac{t}{4}\sin\delta -\frac{1}{2},\] which shows that if $\sin\delta \geq 4/t$ then $(x_i,y_i)\not\in S_{\theta+\delta}$ , which is the control of shared elements we want. To work the details out, since $4/t\lesssim d$ , we can take $\delta \sim d$ while maintaining that $\sin\delta \geq 4/t$ . Let $S_{\theta}'$ be the set of points $(x_i,y_i)$ with $i\geq t/2$ . Define $S_{\theta+k\delta}'$ similarly for all $k=1,\ldots,n=\lfloor\pi/2\delta\rfloor$ . Then by the discussion above, $S_{\theta}$ has empty intersections with $S_{\theta+\delta}',\ldots,S_{\theta+n\delta}'$ . Similarly, $S_{\theta+\delta}'$ has empty intersections with $S_{\theta+2\delta}', \ldots,S_{\theta+n\delta}'$ , and so on. Since each of them has at least $t/2\gtrsim d^{-1}$ elements, and $n\sim \delta^{-1}\sim d^{-1}$ , we know that the union of them has $\gtrsim d^{-2}$ elements. Hence, \[|S|\geq \left|\bigcup_{k=0}^{n}S_{\theta+k\delta}'\right|\gtrsim d^{-2},\] as desired.
Now by Lemma 1. we have $d\gtrsim D/N$ , and by Lemma 2. we have $d^2\gtrsim 1/D$ . Multiplying the two inequalities, we get that $d^3\gtrsim 1/N$ , which shows that $d\gtrsim N^{-1/3}$ .

Original statementThere are $N\geq 2$ points on a plane, each representing a person. Due to an ongoing pandemic, they are required to adhere to the social distancing measures posed by the government. Tbh I didn't think that I could completely resolve this problem (well there is still a $\log N$ gap but who cares). I decided to put this in the remark and suggest that it can be made in the form of 2014 P6, which is the only problem I didn't get $7$ on (and I got $0$ lol). So... treat this as my revenge. You're welcome :D.

Great! The same idea as in #68 but with much simpler implementation. The first case is when the points are "too densely" packed, i.e. when the maximum distance (or the perimeter of the convex hull) is less than  $n^{2/3}.$  In this case we look for a line  $ \ell$  that just chips off a small piece of the convex hull. (because there are "too many" points inside the convex hull and  $\ell$  could have passed near some of them if it were allowed to penetrate deeper). This is the most complicated case.
The second case is when the points are not tightly packed, they are on average too far away from one another, i.e. the maximum distance (or the perimeter of the convex hull) is greater than  $n^{2/3}$ . In this case we project  $ P$  on an appropriate line  $\ell' $  (the line on which  $ P$  has the longest projection) and establish that there exists a line  $ \ell$  that is perpendicular to  $ \ell'$  and does not pass too close to any point. 

I struggled how to implement this idea, because this can be very easily done in case the convex hull has a regular shape, for example when it's close to a circle. So, in #68 the more complicated case was done via some averaging arguments, but it became comparatively lengthy solution, and the main idea was obscured by the technical details. Your approach is much easier and enjoyable!

Just a small note: Do not write \(D\ge O(n^{2/3})\) or \(D\le O(n^{2/3})\), especially the former one. By definition  $D=O(\cdot)$  just means  $D\le c (\cdots)$  for some constant  $c>0$ . If you want to express  $D\ge c(\cdots)$ , there is another notation  $D=\Omega(\cdot)$  But it's enough simply to consider the cases  $D\le n^{2/3}$  and  $D>n^{2/3}$  and adjust the constant inside these cases.**EDIT**. One may ask: where does the threshold  $n^{2/3}$  come from? The motivation behind it is natural. The most common approach to this problem, in my opinion, is to try to project the points on a line  $\ell$  on which the convex hull has the longest projection, say  $D$ . It is easily calculated that we would get the required result only if  $D\ge cn^{2/3}$  where  $c$  can be any constant (but fixed, not depending on  $n$ ). So, obviously when  $D<n^{2/3}$  some other approach has to be found.

From AMSP Combinatorics 3: Pick two points $A, B$ in $\mathcal S$ such that $AB$ is maximal. There are essentially two cases. The first case is when the projections of $\mathcal S$ onto $\overline{AB}$ create two consecutive projections at a distance of $d \geq n^{-\frac 13}$ . In this case, taking the perpendicular bisector of these two projections, say $P'$ and $Q'$ , works (take $c=\frac 12$ and any other point has greater distance to $\ell$ than either $P$ or $Q$ .) Note that the projections are strictly contained inside segment $\overline{AB}$ due to maximality. Now, suppose that all consecutive projections have length less than $n^{-\frac 13} = d$ . Obviously, all the points in $\mathcal S$ must lie inside the circle centered at $B$ with radius $nd$ . Consider a region $\mathcal C$ bounded by a perpendicular to $\overline{AB}$ a fixed distance, say, $\frac 12$ , and the arc formed by the intersection points of the line with the circle (say $C$ and $D$ .) Project the points on $\mathcal S \cap \mathcal C$ onto $\overline{AE}$ , where $E$ is the desired intersection. Running a similar argument, $$ \frac 12 = AE \leq d |\mathcal C \cap \mathcal S|, $$ which implies $$ |\mathcal S \cap \mathcal C| \geq \frac 1{2d}. $$ **Claim.** There are at most $c(M+1)$ points of $\mathcal S$ inside any $1 \times M$ rectangle, where $c$ is a fixed constant. *Proof.* Draw circles of radius $\frac 12$ around every point in $\mathcal S$ ; as all the disks are contained within a larger rectangle with area $(1+1)(1+M) = 2(1+M)$ , we have the bound $$ [\text{Rectangle}] \geq \sum [\mathcal D_i], $$ so the intersection has at most $\frac 8{\pi} (1+M)$ points after the computation. $\blacksquare$ Utilizing the claim, consider the rectangle with width 1 and length equal tp $$ CD=2\sqrt{BC^2-BE^2} = 2\sqrt{AB-\frac 14} < 2\sqrt{AB} \leq 2\sqrt{nd}. $$ Combining the bounds, $$ \frac 1{2d} \leq |\mathcal C \cap \mathcal S| \leq \frac 8{\pi}(1+2\sqrt{nd}). $$ Scaling $d$ down by some large constant (say, $10^6$ ), we achieve a contradiction.

Take a circle  $\Gamma$  of minimal radius containing all of  $\mathcal{S}$  and suppose it has radius  $r$ . Let  $P,Q$  be the points in  $\mathcal{S}$  such that  $PQ$  is maximal, and note that by considering a large circle centered at the midpoint of  $\overline{PQ}$  we have  $r \leq \sqrt{3}PQ$ .

If  $r \geq n^{2/3}$ , we have  $PQ=\Omega(n^{2/3})$  as well. By maximality, the projection of every point onto line  $\overline{PQ}$  lies on segment  $\overline{PQ}$ , which has length  $\Omega(n^{2/3})$ . Thus by expectation there exist some two adjacent projections  $B,C$  such that  $BC=\Omega(n^{-1/3})$ , and taking  $\ell$  to be the perpendicular bisector of  $\overline{BC}$  works, since it separates the segment joining the preimages of  $B$  and  $C$  but has distance at least  $\tfrac{BC}{2}=\Omega(n^{-1/3})$  from every point in  $\mathcal{S}$ .

If  $r \leq n^{2/3}$ , then note that by maximality there exists a point  $A \in \mathcal{S}$  on the circumference of  $\Gamma$ . Let points  $S,T$  lie on  $\Gamma$  such that  $AS=AT$  and  $d(A,\overline{ST})=1$ . Let  $M$  be the midpoint of  $\overline{ST}$  and  $A'$  the  $A$ -antipode. By power of a point, we have  $$ MS\cdot MT=MA\cdot MA'=1\cdot (2r-1)=O(n^{2/3}) \implies ST=O(n^{1/3}). $$  It is clear that not every point in  $\mathcal{S}$  lies in segment  $\widehat{SAT}$  of  $\Gamma$  (for sufficiently large  $n$ ; small  $n$  don't matter), else the circle with diameter  $\overline{ST}$  is (much) smaller and still contains everything.

Now consider a height- $1$  rectangle  $STUV$  such that  $A$  is the midpoint of  $\overline{UV}$ , which has area  $ST=O(n^{1/3})$ . Note that every point on the same side of  $\overline{ST}$  as  $A$  lies in  $STUV$ . I claim that there are  $O(n^{1/3})$  points in  $\mathcal{S}$  in it. Indeed, since all points in  $\mathcal{S}$  have distance at least  $1$  from each other, we may draw an open disc of radius  $\tfrac{1}{2}$  around each, and none of these discs overlap. Every disc associated with a point in  $STUV$  lies completely within the rectangle with width  $ST+1$  and height  $2$  with parallel sides and common center as  $STUV$ , whose area is also  $O(n^{1/3})$ , and since each disc has  $\Omega(1)$  area we must have  $O(n^{1/3})$  discs, as desired.

Now consider projecting every point in  $\mathcal{S}$ , as well as  $T$ , onto the line through  $A$  perpendicular to  $ST$ , and let  $T'$  be the image of  $T'$  under this projection. There are  $O(n^{1/3})$  projected points on segment  $\overline{AT'}$ , which has length  $1$ , hence we may find two adjacent projected points  $B,C$  on this segment such that  $BC=\Omega(n^{-1/3})$ . Then taking  $\ell$  as the perpendicular bisector of  $\overline{BC}$  works, since as before its distance from any point in  $\mathcal{S}$  is at least  $\tfrac{BC}{2}=\Omega(n^{-1/3})$ , and  $\ell$  separates the segment joining  $A$  with some point in  $\mathcal{S}$  on the other side of line  $\overline{ST}$ , which we previously proved exists. This finishes the problem.  $\blacksquare$

Let  $c$  be a sufficiently small constant. Assume  $n$  is sufficiently high. Assume toward a contradiction there is no line separating  $S$  such that the distance from the line to any point is at least  $\frac c2 n^{-1/3}$ .

Let  $A$  be one of the points.

Claim: No point is more than  $cn^{2/3}$  units from  $A$ .
Proof: Assume toward a contradiction some point  $B$  is more than  $cn^{2/3}$  units away from  $A$ . Project all of the points onto line  $AB$  to get a set  $S'$  of points. Then, on this line there must be a segment of length  $cn^{-1/3}$  between  $A$  and  $B$  with no elements of  $S'$ . The perpendicular bisector of that segment has distance at least  $\frac c2 n^{-1/3}$  from each point in  $S$ .

Let  $P$  be the point in  $S$  with the highest distance from  $A$ . Assume  $A$  is at position  $(0, 0)$  and  $P$  is at position  $(d, 0)$ .

Let  $T$  be the set of points in  $S$  with  $x$  coordinate over  $d-1$ .

Let  $(x, y)\in T$ . Then,  $x^2+y^2\le d^2$ , so  $y^2\le x^2-d^2 \le 2d-1$ . Therefore,  $y\le \sqrt{2d-1}$ .

So,  $T$  is contained in the rectangle bounded by  $x>d-1$ ,  $x\le d$ ,  $y\le \sqrt{2d-1}$ ,  $y\ge -\sqrt{2d-1}$ . Therefore, there are at most  $2\sqrt{2d-1}+1 \le 2\sqrt{2c}n^{1/3} + 1$  points in  $T$ .

Because there is a point with  $x$  coordinate exactly  $d$ , by pigeonhole, there is some interval of length at least  $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{c}n^{1/3}+1} \ge cn^{-1/3}$  within  $[d, d+1]$  such that no point in  $T$  has an  $x$  coordinate in that interval. Let that interval be  $(a, b)$ . Then, the line  $x=\frac{a+b}2$  has distance at least  $\frac c2 n^{-1/3}$  from each point in  $S$ .

Let $d=AB$ for $A,B \in \mathcal S$ be a chord with maximal distance, now consider the area that bounds $\mathcal S$ which is $(A,AB) \cap (B,BA)$ , the reason for this pick is that in order to get bounds it's ideal to have all points on $\mathcal S$ down control enclosed in a convex shape, it's not the first time I see this idea but in a previous one it ended up not being needed, unlike here where it's literaly awesome. Our idea will be that, we project the points on a line $\ell'$ and then if we get that two consecutive projections make a distance of $O(n^{-\frac{1}{3}})$ we are simply done by letting $\ell$ to be perp bisector of these two points chosen, and it makes sense to start focusing through here, as it's the best way to handle the distances condition without embracing the chaos, to simply put it all in parallel lines to measure their distance, also another reason to pick maximal $AB$ as you get that all are inside the segment and can control the projections by taking maximal, which is what we will do now. If we had that $d \ge O(n^{\frac{2}{3}})$ then let the projections to $AB$ from the points of $\mathcal S$ in consecutive order starting from $A$ be $A=P_1, P_2, \cdots, P_{n-1}, P_n=B$ then take maximal $P_iP_{i+1}$ which is at least $\frac{d}{n-1} \ge O(n^{-\frac{1}{3}})$ which wins by the observations made above. Now what if $d \le O(n^{\frac{2}{3}})$ , in this case we follow the insight that if they aren't too separate then we have a couple of stacked points in one single region, but what could it be?, we want to ensure that this region also contains the projections in order for us to measure them on $AB$ , therefore by parallel lines, this suggests a rectangle, from the idea of pushing points into one place if they aren't too far apart, we conclude that it would be good to have one side constant (more specifically to be $1$ ) as now we can do this:**Claim:** On a $1 \times g$ we have that there is at most $O(g)$ points from $\mathcal S$ on it.**Proof:** Consider from each point a circle with radius $0.5$ , none of the circles intersect clearly from the condition so now since at least a quarter of their area is in $1 \times g$ we have that there can be at most $\frac{16g}{\pi}$ circles on the rectangle, so since each was from a unique point then it's just $O(g)$ points in $1 \times g$ at most, thus the claim is proven. And now the way we use this is that if we let $L$ between $A,B$ on $AB$ such that $AL=1$ and $K$ be midpoint of $AL$ , then consider the perpendicular from $K$ to $AB$ to hit $(B,BA)$ at $C,D$ (clearly its inside the convex bound of $\mathcal S$ as $d \ge 1$ ), so by pythagorean theorem we have that $CD=2\sqrt{d^2-(d-0.5)^2}=O(\sqrt{d}) \le O(n^{\frac{1}{3}})$ , so if you consider the rectangle formed by the lines $A\infty_{\perp AB}, L \infty_{\perp AB}, C\infty_{AB}, D \infty_{AB}$ then this is a $1 \times CD$ which then from the bound above and the claim contains at most $O(n^{\frac{1}{3}})$ points, if it contained zero we take $CD$ as $\ell$ , and win trivially, else let $A=R_0, R_1, \cdots R_{m-1}$ be inside the rectangle and let $R_m$ be the point outside the rectangle such that its projection to $AB$ its the closest to $L$ , then we apply the same insight from the beggining and consider the maximal $R_iR_{i+1}$ which is at least $\frac{1}{m}$ and oh suprice, from the $O$ bounds above this is at least $O(n^{-\frac{1}{3}})$ which completes this case. Since in both cases such line $\ell$ exists, we are done :cool:.

Let  $O$  be the circumcenter of the smallest circle containing all  $n$  points. If the circumradius is at least  $10^{-10}n^{2/3}$ , then we claim there are two points with distance at least  $10^{-10}n^{2/3}$ . If the circumcircle contains two points, it must be a diameter, so the distance is  $2\cdot10^{-10}n^{2/3}$ . Otherwise, the circumcircle must contain points forming a polygon containing  $O$ , so it contains some acute triangle. The longest side is at least  $\sqrt3\cdot10^{-10}n^{2/3}$ . Then, rotate such that those two points form a horizontal line. Project onto the  $x$ -axis. Some distance between two consecutive points must be at least  $10^{-10}n^{-1/3}$ , so there exists a separating line with minimal distance at least  $\frac12\cdot10^{-10}n^{-1/3}$ .

Otherwise, the circumradius is less than  $10^{-10}n^{2/3}$ . Let the radius be  $r$ . Let  $A$  be the point furthest away from  $O$ . Consider the line through  $A$  perpendicular to  $OA$ . Consider the region of points at most  $0.25$  from this line. The maximum distance from any point in  $\mathcal S$  that is inside this region to  $OA$  is at most  $\sqrt{r^2-(r-0.25)^2}\leq\sqrt{0.5r}\leq10^{-5}n^{1/3}$ . Therefore, since any two points in  $\mathcal S$  in this region must have  $y$ -coordinates which differ by at least  $0.8$ , there are at most  $10^{-4}n^{1/3}$  points in  $\mathcal S$  in this region. Then, project the points in  $\mathcal S$  onto  $OA$ . There are at most  $10^{-4}n^{1/3}$  points projected within  $0.25$  of the projection of  $A$ , so there exists a line that is at least  $10^3n^{-1/3}$  away from all  $n$  points.

stem_md:
Two squirrels, Bushy and Jumpy, have collected 2021 walnuts for the winter. Jumpy numbers the walnuts from 1 through 2021, and digs 2021 little holes in a circular pattern in the ground around their favourite tree. The next morning Jumpy notices that Bushy had placed one walnut into each hole, but had paid no attention to the numbering. Unhappy, Jumpy decides to reorder the walnuts by performing a sequence of 2021 moves. In the  $k$ -th move, Jumpy swaps the positions of the two walnuts adjacent to walnut  $k$ .

Prove that there exists a value of  $k$  such that, on the  $k$ -th move, Jumpy swaps some walnuts  $a$  and  $b$  such that  $a<k<b$ .
solution_md:
This is overdue by 33 days! The only problem I solved in this IMO which isn't P1 or P4. 

Haven't seen this Solution anywhere in this thread and the official Sol --- though it resembles Sol 4 (albeit this being a bit simpler).
--------
First, I will introduce some notations as below: $\color{green} \rule{7.4cm}{2pt}$   $\color{green} \clubsuit$   $\boxed{\textbf{All Equally Directed = Impossible.}}$   $\color{green} \clubsuit$   $\color{green} \rule{7.4cm}{2pt}$  
In a circular configuration of  $2021$  numbers, call a number to be  $\color{green} \textbf{\textit{equally directed}}$  if it is either greater or less than both its neighbors. Furthermore, name it  $\color{green} \textbf{\textit{relatively-humongous}}$  or  $\color{green} \textbf{\textit{relatively-tiny}}$ , respectively. (The distinction is intentionally made extreme and polarizing) 

Moving from the individual or local numbers to the whole config, call a configuration to be  $\color{green} \textbf{\textit{double-arrow}}$  if all its  $2021$  numbers are equally directed. 

We Claim that there are no double-arrow configurations.   $\color{green} \rule{25cm}{0.2pt}$   $\color{green} \spadesuit$   $\boxed{\textbf{Proof.}}$   $\color{green} \spadesuit$  
This isn't hard; put the sign  $>$  or  $<$  between each neighboring pair of numbers. Since all numbers are equally oriented, the signs alternate. This is impossible since there are  $2021$  signs, arranged circularly.  $\color{green} \rule{25cm}{0.2pt}$  
Following what basically everyone does, assume FTSOC that no walnut  $k$  exists. 

Now, we introduce  $\color{red} \textbf{\textit{three}}$  new squirrels, whose names are Photy, Dreamy and Stoppy. We also group them into two teams (with Bushy being neutral) as follows:
[list = disc] [*] put Jumpy and Photy to the  $\color{red} \textbf{\textit{real}}$  team, and [*] put Dreamy and Stoppy to the  $\color{red} \textbf{\textit{fantasy}}$  team. Additionally, the fantasy team will have 2021 holes in another circular-tree of choice. [/list]

We also describe their function here:
[list = disc] [*] Bushy places the same order of walnuts in both trees, [*] Jumpy's job is unchanged, [*] Photy's job is to take photos of the  $2021+1$  different moments, captioning the photos with  $P_i$  ( $0 \leq i \leq 2021$ ). Assuming the contradiction, Photy also records whether walnut  $k$  ( $1 \leq k \leq 2021$ ) is relatively-tiny or relatively-humongous with respect to  $P_k$ . [/list]
Switching over to the fantasy team,  
[list = disc] [*] In each  $k$  ( $1 \leq k \leq 2021$ ), Dreamy is to look at Photy's observation of  $k$ 's standing; if  $k$  is rel-tiny, he tells Stoppy to stop; and if humongous, to swap. (As a bonus, he also records dreamingly of  $Q_i$   $(0 \leq i \leq 2021)$ , mimicking Photy's actions) [*] Following that, Stoppy becomes lazy on hearing  $\textit{stop}$  and performs Jumpy's move on hearing  $\textit{swap}$ . [/list]

Our interest will be on Stoppy's actions (which are supported by Photy's and Dreamy's transmission of information) with respect to Jumpy.  $\color{red} \rule{4.4cm}{2pt}$   $\color{red} \clubsuit$   $\color{red} \boxed{\textbf{Qhantom Qosition.}}$   $\color{red} \clubsuit$   $\color{red} \rule{4.4cm}{2pt}$  
In each turn, 
[list = disc] [*]  $Q_k$ 's  $k$ -walnut will have the same position as  $P_k$ 's walnut (meaning Stoppy will look at the same place as Jumpy does); and [*]  $Q_k$ 's  $k$ -walnut will be equally directed with the same orientation as  $P_k$ 's (of course, assuming the contradiction). [/list] $\color{red} \rule{25cm}{0.2pt}$   $\color{red} \spadesuit$   $\color{red} \boxed{\textbf{Qroof.}}$   $\color{red} \spadesuit$  
The proof is done inductively: fix a number  $k$ , and assume both statements are true for numbers  $k-1$  or less. We prove the former bullet point first: 

Observe that in each  $i$ -th Jumpy or Stoppy's move, the  $k$ -walnut will move the same way every time. This is because  $k$  is in the same place in  $P_0$  and  $Q_0$ ; and assuming they are at the same place at  $P_i,Q_i$   $(0 \leq i \leq k-2)$ , they will move if and only if the walnut  $i+1$  is located beside them. 

As we know that the walnut  $i+1$  lies at the same place in  $P_{i+1}$  and  $Q_{i+1}$ .  $\blacksquare$  

<details><summary>Notes 1.</summary>The same reasoning could be applied to prove that walnut  $K$  will occupy the same position in  $P_k$  and  $Q_k$ , for  $K \geq k$ . 

While this observation is not needed for the proofs to come, it's a good visualizer to imagine  $P_k$  and  $Q_k$ 's relationship.</details>
--------
Next, the latter bullet point:

in  $P_k$  and  $Q_k$ , Bushy performs the additional job (only for now) to eat all walnuts  $1$  to  $k-1$  and leave their seeds in their place (synonymous with the official Sol's wording of such walnuts being  $\color{red} \textbf{\textit{used}}$ ). Assume that all seeds are identical. 

We prove the stronger statement that the seeds of  $1$  to  $k-1$  occupy the same position globally. If this is so, since walnut  $k$ 's number is greater than all the seeds' hypothetical number, then  $k$ 's relatively-tiny and relatively-humongous properties carry over from  $P_k$  to  $Q_k$ . 

(Note how the tiny and humongous wording functions here.) 

This is also provable by induction. If  $1$  to  $k-1$ 's seeds occupy the same places, since  $k$  lies at the same place, then the set of  $1$  to  $k$ 's seeds are equal too.  $\blacksquare$   $\blacksquare$  

(In any case, whether Stoppy stops of swaps in  $Q_{k-1}$ , assuming that seeds are swapped with seeds and walnuts are swapped with walnuts, the  $\color{red} \textbf{\textit{sets}}$  will not change.) 
--------
Now undo Bushy's job of turning used walnuts into seeds. We relate Stoppy's hypothetical position to the green Claim for the ultimate contradiction: $\color{blue} \rule{4.2cm}{2pt}$   $\color{blue} \clubsuit$   $\color{blue} \boxed{\textbf{Qhantom Qower.}}$   $\color{blue} \clubsuit$   $\color{blue} \rule{4.2cm}{2pt}$  
We Claim that in  $Q_k$ , the numbers  $1$  to  $k$  are equally directed.

Call  $a,c$  the neighbors of this triplet and define the *small neighbor* to be  $\text{min}(a,c)$ . Let's see what happens to ordered triplets. Let  $a,b,c,d,e$  be in this order with  $a,b,c$  triplet right before iteration  $d$ . The only way we can change an ordered triplet is by swapping exactly one of its neighbors or its center. Now we swap  $c$  at iteration  $d$ . Clearly,  $c,d,e$  cannot be a triplet so their order relations relative to themselves remain unchanged. 
If the order relation between  $b$  and  $e$  is the same as the order relation between  $b$  and  $c$  then the center of this triplet is the same and we say the triplet *perturbed*.

Then the acorns  $1,2,\dots,k$  partition the rest of the acorn into nonempty contiguous runs (each of which only contains acorns among  $k+1,k+2,\dots,n$ ). Now consider the  $(k+1)$ th move. Otherwise, the acorn is in a run of length greater than  $1$ , say,  $x$ , in which case it cannot be one of the  $2$  acorns at the edge of the run. Then the run is split into runs of length  $y,z>0$  with  $y+z=x-1$ .

After the  $1$ st move, we are left with a single run of length  $n-1$ , which is even. We now show that there is always a nonzero run of even length after the first move. So, a nonzero even run always exists.

Now, at the end of the process, there are no runs left. However, we showed that a nonzero even run always exists. This is a contradiction, as desired.</details>

stem_md: Show that the inequality \[\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \sqrt{|x_i-x_j|}\leqslant \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \sqrt{|x_i+x_j|}\]holds for all real numbers  $x_1,\ldots x_n.$

solutionWe will use the following result: $$ |x|^\alpha \sim \int_0^\infty \frac{1-\cos (xt)}{t^{1+\alpha}}dt \, , $$ and in particular for $\alpha = \frac{1}{2}$ we have $$ \sqrt{|x|}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_0^\infty \frac{1-\cos(xt)}{t^{\frac{3}{2}}} dt \, . $$ For our problem, this means \begin{align*} \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \left(\sqrt{|x_i+x_j|}-\sqrt{|x_i-x_j|}\right) &= \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_0^\infty \frac{(1-\cos((x_i+x_j)t))-(1-\cos((x_i-x_j)t)}{t^{\frac{3}{2}}} dt\right) &=\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_0^\infty\frac{\cos(x_it-x_jt)-\cos(x_it+x_jt)}{t^{\frac{3}{2}}} dt\right) &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_0^\infty\frac{1}{t^{\frac{3}{2}}}\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n 2\sin(x_it)\sin(x_jt) \, dt &= \frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_0^\infty\frac{1}{t^{\frac{3}{2}}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n \sin(x_it)\right)^2 \, dt \geq 0 \, . \end{align*} This concludes the problem. $\square$

Let $f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \sqrt{|(x_i+x)+(x_j+x)|}$ . We have $\lim_{x_\to\infty}=\lim_{x_\to-\infty}=\infty$ and $f$ ist continuous. Thus there is an $x$ for which $f(x)$ ist minimal. Since $\sqrt{x}$ ist convex, $f(x)$ is minimal for $2x=x_i+x_j$ . For $i=j$ we can reduce the inequality to $n-1$ variables. For $i\neq j$ we can reduce the inequality to $n-2$ variables.

First we note that adding a constant  $\frac{y}{2}$  to all the variables  $x_i$  doesn't change the LHS. So we might try to do this in a way that makes the RHS smaller. If we can prove the resulting (stronger) inequality, we will be done, and according to the problem statement, it should still hold, so this seems like a promising plan.

Each term on the RHS will now be of the form  $\sqrt{|x_i + x_j + y|}$ , and so the derivative with respect to  $y$  is   $$ \frac{sgn(x_i + x_j + y)}{\sqrt{|x_i + x_j + y|}} $$  for any  $y$  such that  $x_i + x_j + y \neq 0$ . Note that this is strictly strictly decreasing for  $y < - x_i - x_j$  \textit{and} for  $y > -x_i - x_j$ . (Here we show a proof using calculus, but it's possible to do it without this using that square root is concave).

The derivative of the entire sum on the RHS is the sum of the derivatives, so it is also strictly decreasing in any interval such that  $x_i + x_j + y \neq 0$  for all  $i,j$ . If the (total) derivative is positive, the RHS is currently increasing in  $y$ , so picking a small negative  $y$  will decrease the RHS. In fact, since the derivative is strictly decreasing, we can keep making  $y$  smaller until we hit a point where  $y = -x_i-x_j$  for some  $i,j$ , and the RHS will only decrease faster and faster since the derivative becomes larger and larger as  $y$  decreases. Conversely, if the (total) derivative is negative we should pick a small positive  $y$  and then keep increasing it until  $y = -x_i - x_j$  for some  $i,j$ . In the special case where the derivative is zero we can in fact move in any direction (we will be at a local maximum), and we will then keep moving in this direction, again because the derivative is strictly decreasing.

The above argument shows that it's enough to consider a case where there is some  $i,j$  such that  $x_i = - x_j$ . But then just plugging in these values into the inequality we notice that every term involving  $x_i$  or  $x_j$  cancels (this is easy to check). Hence we have reduced it to showing the inequality for  $n-2$  numbers  $x_1, ..., x_{n-2}$ .

We can now finish by induction. It only remains to check the base cases  $n = 0$  and  $n = 1$  which are both trivial.

<details><summary>Comment</summary>Note that the only thing we used about the square roots is that they are concave on the intervals where  $y \neq - x_i - x_j$ . And in fact the inequality holds if we replace the square roots by any concave function on the positive reals - the proof is identical. We can also use this insight to reformulate the proof without mention of any derivatives or calculus using the well-known properties of concave functions that a sum of concave functions is concave and that a concave function can only achieve its minimum on an interval at the endpoints. This should be very intuitive: just draw a "sad face". And much of the inspiration for solving this problem is coming exactly from drawing the graph of  $\sqrt{|x|}$  and thinking about what happens when you move points.</details>

Here's an elementary solution. If $x_i = 0$ for some $i$ , WLOG $x_n = 0$ . Then by induction on $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{n - 1})$ , \begin{align*} \sum_{1 \le i,j \le n} \sqrt{|x_i + x_j|} &= 2 \cdot \sum_{1 \le i \le n - 1} \sqrt{|x_i|} + \sum_{1 \le i ,j \le n - 1} \sqrt{|x_i + x_{j}|} &\ge 2 \cdot \sum_{1 \le i \le n - 1} \sqrt{|x_i|} + \sum_{1 \le i ,j \le n- 1} \sqrt{|x_i - x_j|} &= \sum_{1 \le i,j \le n} \sqrt{|x_i - x_j|} \end{align*} Otherwise, we could assume that $x_i \not= 0$ for all $i$ , and therefore, $\sqrt{|x_i + x_j|} + \sqrt{|x_i - x_j|} > 0$ for all $i,j$ , then WLOG $|x_1| \le |x_2| \le |x_3| \le \dots \le |x_n|$ , and define $y_i = |x_{i}| - |x_{i - 1}|$ , where $x_0 = 0$ . Also, write $x_i = \varepsilon_i |x_i|$ for all $i$ . \begin{align*} \sum_i \sum_j \sqrt{|x_i + x_j|} - \sqrt{|x_i - x_j|} &= \sum_i \sum_j \frac{|x_i + x_j| - |x_i - x_j|}{\sqrt{|x_i + x_j|} + \sqrt{x_i - x_j|}} &= 2 \sum_i \sum_j \frac{\varepsilon_i \varepsilon_j \min(|x_i|,|x_j|)}{\sqrt{|x_i + x_j|} + \sqrt{|x_i - x_j|} } &\ge \frac{2}{\max_{i,j} \sqrt{|x_i + x_j|} + \sqrt{|x_i - x_j|}} \left( \sum_i \sum_j \varepsilon_i \varepsilon_j \min(|x_i|,|x_j|) \right) &\ge \frac{2}{\max_{i,j} \sqrt{|x_i + x_j|} + \sqrt{|x_i - x_j|}} \left( \sum_i \sum_j \varepsilon_i \varepsilon_j \sum_{k \le \min(i,j)} y_k \right) &= \frac{2}{\max_{i,j} \sqrt{|x_i + x_j|} + \sqrt{|x_i - x_j|}} \left( \sum_k y_k \sum_{i,j \ge k} \varepsilon_i \varepsilon_j \right) &= \frac{2}{\max_{i,j} \sqrt{|x_i + x_j|} + \sqrt{|x_i - x_j|}} \left( \sum_k y_k \left( \sum_{i \ge k} \varepsilon_i \right)^2 \right) &\ge 0 \end{align*}

The idea is to force \(x_i+x_j=0\) for some \(i\), \(j\), then induct down. **Claim:** If \(x_i+x_j\ne0\) for all \(i\), \(j\), then for some \(k\) the sequence \(x_1+k\), \ldots, \(x_n+k\) produces the same left-hand side but a smaller right-hand side. *Proof.* Evidently shifting the \(x_i\) by a constant does not affect the left-hand side. Take small $\varepsilon$ , and observe by Jensen that \[ \left(\sum_{i,j}\sqrt{|x_i+x_j+2\varepsilon|}+\sqrt{|x_i+x_j-2\varepsilon|}\right) \le\sum_{i,j}2\sqrt{|x_i+x_j|}, \] so either \[\sum_{i,j}\sqrt{|x_i+x_j+2\varepsilon|}\le\sum_{i,j}\sqrt{|x_i+x_j|}\quad\text{or}\quad\sum_{i,j}\sqrt{|x_i+x_j-2\varepsilon|}\le\sum_{i,j}\sqrt{|x_i+x_j|}.\] Thus either \(k=\varepsilon\) or \(k=-\varepsilon\) works. \(\blacksquare\) Therefore we reduce the problem to the cases where \(x_i+x_j=0\) for some \(i\), \(j\). Finally, deleting \(x_i=+x\) and \(x_j=-x\) decreases both sides by \[2\sqrt{2x}+\sum_{k\ne i,j}\left(2\sqrt{|x_k-x|}+2\sqrt{|x_k+x|}\right),\] so we may induct down. The remaining base cases of \(n=0,1\) are trivial. **Remark:** The above proof shows that the equality cases of this inequality are when the \(x_i\) are symmetric across 0.

\[= 2\cdot \sum_{k=1}^n \sqrt{|x_i+x_k|}+2\cdot \sum_{k=1}^n \sqrt{|x_j+x_k|}-\sqrt{|x_i+x_i|} -\sqrt{|x_j+x_j|}-2\sqrt{x_i+x_j}\]
Then, by the inductive hypothesis the inequality holds on what is left, so 
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n-2}\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}\sqrt{|x_i-x_j|}\leq \sum_{i=1}^{n-2}\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}\sqrt{|x_i+x_j|}\]
summed with our previous equality, we've now proved the inequality and we're done  $\blacksquare$ .

Show that the inequality \[\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \sqrt{|x_i-x_j|}\leqslant \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \sqrt{|x_i+x_j|}\]holds for all real numbers $x_1,\ldots x_n.$
Here's an elementary solution. If $x_i = 0$ for some $i$ , WLOG $x_n = 0$ . Then by induction on $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{n - 1})$ , \begin{align*} \sum_{1 \le i,j \le n} \sqrt{|x_i + x_j|} &= 2 \cdot \sum_{1 \le i \le n - 1} \sqrt{|x_i|} + \sum_{1 \le i ,j \le n - 1} \sqrt{|x_i + x_{j}|} &\ge 2 \cdot \sum_{1 \le i \le n - 1} \sqrt{|x_i|} + \sum_{1 \le i ,j \le n- 1} \sqrt{|x_i - x_j|} &= \sum_{1 \le i,j \le n} \sqrt{|x_i - x_j|} \end{align*} Otherwise, we could assume that $x_i \not= 0$ for all $i$ , and therefore, $\sqrt{|x_i + x_j|} + \sqrt{|x_i - x_j|} > 0$ for all $i,j$ , then WLOG $|x_1| \le |x_2| \le |x_3| \le \dots \le |x_n|$ , and define $y_i = |x_{i}| - |x_{i - 1}|$ , where $x_0 = 0$ . Also, write $x_i = \varepsilon_i |x_i|$ for all $i$ . \begin{align*} \sum_i \sum_j \sqrt{|x_i + x_j|} - \sqrt{|x_i - x_j|} &= \sum_i \sum_j \frac{|x_i + x_j| - |x_i - x_j|}{\sqrt{|x_i + x_j|} + \sqrt{x_i - x_j|}} &= 2 \sum_i \sum_j \frac{\varepsilon_i \varepsilon_j \min(|x_i|,|x_j|)}{\sqrt{|x_i + x_j|} + \sqrt{|x_i - x_j|} } &\ge \frac{2}{\max_{i,j} \sqrt{|x_i + x_j|} + \sqrt{|x_i - x_j|}} \left( \sum_i \sum_j \varepsilon_i \varepsilon_j \min(|x_i|,|x_j|) \right) &\ge \frac{2}{\max_{i,j} \sqrt{|x_i + x_j|} + \sqrt{|x_i - x_j|}} \left( \sum_i \sum_j \varepsilon_i \varepsilon_j \sum_{k \le \min(i,j)} y_k \right) &= \frac{2}{\max_{i,j} \sqrt{|x_i + x_j|} + \sqrt{|x_i - x_j|}} \left( \sum_k y_k \sum_{i,j \ge k} \varepsilon_i \varepsilon_j \right) &= \frac{2}{\max_{i,j} \sqrt{|x_i + x_j|} + \sqrt{|x_i - x_j|}} \left( \sum_k y_k \left( \sum_{i \ge k} \varepsilon_i \right)^2 \right) &\ge 0 \end{align*}

Straightforward integral bash : Let  $X,Y$  be i.i.d. random variables then   $$  \mathbb{E}|X+Y|^{\frac{1}{2}}\ge \mathbb{E}|X-Y|^{\frac{1}{2}} $$  Actually we are going to prove something more: If  $\phi:[0,+\infty)\to \mathbb{R}$  is continuous in its domain and twice differentiable in  $(0,+\infty)$  and such that  $\phi(0)=0$  , is **increasing(positive)** , **concave** and **eventually constant** then   $$ \mathbb{E}(\phi(|X+Y|))\ge \mathbb{E}(\phi(|X-Y|)) $$  First we are going to prove that in the case where  $X,Y$  are compactly supported  $X,Y\in [-M,M]$  and to steer clear of  many technical difficulties assume that  $X$  is abslolutely continuous with p.d.f.  $p$ .
So we need to prove that   $$ \int\int \phi(|x+y|) p(x)p(y)dxdy\ge \int\int \phi(|x-y|)p(x)p(y)dxdy $$   Through a change of variables  $s=x+y$  the L.H.S. becomes  $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int \phi(|s|)p(x)p(s-x)dxds=\int_0^{\infty}\phi(s) \int p(x)(p(s-x)+p(-s-x))dx ds$  
and through  $s=y-x$  the R.H.S. becomes    $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int \phi(|s|)p(x)p(x+s)dxds=\int_0^{\infty}\phi(s) \int p(x)(p(x+s)+p(x-s))dx ds$  
So we need to prove that   $$ \int_0^{\infty}\phi(s) \int p(x)(p(s-x)+p(-s-x)-p(s+x)-p(-s+x))dx ds \ge 0 $$  Let  $X$  have cumulative distribution function  $F$  we know that  $F'=p$  almost everywhere. Through an integration by parts the above equals   $$ [\phi(s)(\int p(x)(F(s-x)-F(-s-x)-F(s+x)+F(-s+x))]_{s=0}^{\infty}- $$     $$ -\int_0^{\infty}\phi'(s)(\int p(x)(F(s-x)-F(-s-x)-F(s+x)+F(-s+x))dx)ds $$  the first term above is  $0$  because when  $s>2M$  we have either  $p(x)=0$  or  $ F(s-x)-F(s+x)-F(-s-x)+F(-s+x)=0$  in the second term rewrite the convolutions by suitable changes of variables to arrive at:   $$ -\int_0^{\infty}\phi'(s)(\int F(x)(p(s-x)-p(-s-x)+p(s+x)-p(-s+x))dx)ds= $$   and do an integration by parts again (but this time is more subtle) :  $$ [-\phi'(s)(\int F(x)(F(s-x)+F(-s-x)+F(s+x)+F(-s+x)-2F(x)-2F(-x))dx]_{s=0}^{\infty}+ $$     $$ +\int_0^{\infty}\phi''(s)(\int F(x)(F(s-x)+F(-s-x)+F(s+x)+F(-s+x)-2F(x)-2F(-x))dxds $$  Notice we added  $-2F(x)-2F(-x)$  in the parenthesis and the integrals are well defined cause the term inside them  $F(x)(F(s-x)-F(-x)+F(-s-x)-F(-x)+F(s+x)-F(x)+F(-s+x)-F(x))$  is zero when  $|x|>M+s$  and since  $\phi'(s)=0$  eventually the first term is zero. 
Hereby we have derived the equality   $$ \mathbb{E}(\phi(|X+Y|))-\mathbb{E}(\phi(|X-Y|))=\int_0^{\infty}\phi''(s)(\int F(x)(F(s-x)+F(-s-x)+F(s+x)+F(-s+x)-2F(x)-2F(-x))dxds $$   and we did this assuming absolute continuity but we could have done otherwise so the above holds for any compactly supported random variables . Since  $\phi''\le 0$  all it reamains to  do is show that   $$ \int F(x)(F(s-x)+F(-s-x)+F(s+x)+F(-s+x)-2F(x)-2F(-x))dx\le 0 $$      $$ \int F(x)(F(s-x)-F(-x))+F(x)(F(-s-x)-F(-x))+F(x)(F(s+x)-F(x))+F(x)(F(-s+x)-F(x))dx= $$    $$ =\int F(-x)(F(s+x)-F(x))+F(-s-x)(F(x)-F(s+x))+F(x)(F(s+x)-F(x))+F(s+x)(F(x)-F(s+x)))dx= $$     $$ =-\int (F(x)- F(s+x))(F(-x)-F(-s-x)+F(x)-F(s+x))dx=(x\to -x-s) $$    $$ =-\int(F(-x)-F(-s-x))(F(-x)-F(-s-x)+F(x)-F(s+x))dx=  $$   (and add the latter two to get:)  $$ =-\frac{1}{2}\int (F(-x)-F(-x-s)+F(x)-F(s+x))^2dx \le 0 $$   done. Last but not least we have proved the inequality for bounded random variables to get the general case truncate variables by  $M$  and then send  $M\to \infty$  and use the dominated convergence theorem .  $\sqrt{x}$  is not eventually constant but you can assume that  $|X|\le 1$  due to homogenity and then make the square root constant after some point.

Through an integration by parts the above equals $$ [\phi(s)(\int p(x)(F(s-x)-F(-s-x)-F(s+x)+F(-s+x))]_{s=0}^{\infty}-\int_0^{\infty}\phi'(s)(\int p(x)(F(s-x)-F(-s-x)-F(s+x)+F(-s+x))dx)ds $$ the first term above is $0$ because when $s>2M$ we have either $p(x)=0$ or $ F(s-x)-F(s+x)-F(-s-x)+F(-s+x)=0$ in the second term rewrite the convolutions by suitable changes of variables to arrive at: $$ -\int_0^{\infty}\phi'(s)(\int F(x)(p(s-x)-p(-s-x)+p(s+x)-p(-s+x))dx)ds= $$ and do an integration by parts again (but this time is more subtle) : $$ [-\phi'(s)(\int F(x)(F(s-x)+F(-s-x)+F(s+x)+F(-s+x)-2F(x)-2F(-x))dx]_{s=0}^{\infty}+\int_0^{\infty}\phi''(s)(\int F(x)(F(s-x)+F(-s-x)+F(s+x)+F(-s+x)-2F(x)-2F(-x))dxds $$ Notice we added $-2F(x)-2F(-x)$ in the parenthesis and the integrals are well defined cause the term inside them $F(x)(F(s-x)-F(-x)+F(-s-x)-F(-x)+F(s+x)-F(x)+F(-s+x)-F(x))$ is zero when $|x|>M+s$ and since $\phi'(s)=0$ eventually the first term is zero. Hereby we have derived the equality $$ \mathbb{E}(\phi(X+Y))-\mathbb{E}(\phi(X-Y))=\int_0^{\infty}\phi''(s)(\int F(x)(F(s-x)+F(-s-x)+F(s+x)+F(-s+x)-2F(x)-2F(-x))dxds $$ and we did this assuming absolute continuity but we could have done otherwise so the above holds for any compactly supported random variables . Since $\phi''\le 0$ all it reamains to do is show that $$ \int F(x)(F(s-x)+F(-s-x)+F(s+x)+F(-s+x)-2F(x)-2F(-x))dx\le 0 $$ $$ \int F(x)(F(s-x)-F(-x))+F(x)(F(-s-x)-F(-x))+F(x)(F(s+x)-F(x))+F(x)(F(-s+x)-F(x))dx= $$ $$ =\int F(-x)(F(s+x)-F(x))+F(-s-x)(F(x)-F(s+x))+F(x)(F(s+x)-F(x))+F(s+x)(F(x)-F(s+x)))dx= $$ $$ =-\int (F(x)- F(s+x))(F(-x)-F(-s-x)+F(x)-F(s+x))dx=(x\to -x-s) $$ $$ =-\int(F(-x)-F(-s-x))(F(-x)-F(-s-x)+F(x)-F(s+x))dx= $$ (and add the latter two to get:) $$ =-\frac{1}{2}\int (F(-x)-F(-x-s)+F(x)-F(s+x))^2dx \le 0 $$ done. Last but not least we have proved the inequality for bounded random variables to get the general case truncate variables by $M$ and then send $M\to \infty$ and use the dominted convergence theorem . $\sqrt{x}$ is not eventually constant but you can assume that $|X|\le 1$ due to homogenity and then make the square root constant after some point.

This solution treats the most general case : Let $X,Y$ be i.i.d. random variables then $$ \mathbb{E}|X+Y|^{\frac{1}{2}}\ge \mathbb{E}|X-Y|^{\frac{1}{2}} $$
This can actually be deduced from the original IMO problem by sampling, assuming that $|X|^{1/2}$ is integrable so $|X+Y|^{1/2},|X-Y|^{1/2}\le|X|^{1/2}+|Y|^{1/2}$ are as well. Consider independent samples $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ from $X$ . We have that \[\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n|X_i-X_j|^{1/2}\le\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n|X_i+X_j|^{1/2}.\] Taking expectations on both sides, we have that \[n(n-1)\mathbb E|X-Y|^{1/2}\le n\mathbb E|2X|^{1/2}+n(n-1)\mathbb E|X+Y|^{1/2}.\] Dividing both sides by $n(n-1)$ gives \[\mathbb E|X-Y|^{1/2}\le\mathbb E|X+Y|^{1/2}+\frac{\mathbb E|2X|^{1/2}}{n-1},\] so the result follows by taking the limit as $n\rightarrow\infty$ .

According to the official solutions it is also true that \[\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n|x_i-x_j|^\alpha\le\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n|x_i+x_j|^\alpha\] for all $\alpha\in(0,2]$ . The above solutions work for all $\alpha\le1$ but concavity breaks for $\alpha>1$ . That case seems to require more non-elementary machinery.
Now that this generalisation is mentioned let me provide a proof (with college machinery, of course): it suffices to show for positive reals $x_1,...,x_n,$ \[((x_i+x_j)^\alpha-|x_i-x_j|^\alpha)_{1\leq i,j\leq n}\] is always positive semi-definite. Think of the entries as $((x_i+x_j)^2)^{\alpha/2}-((x_i-x_j)^2)^{\alpha/2}$ and take Taylor expansions, we have \begin{align*} (x_i+x_j)^\alpha-|x_i-x_j|^\alpha&=(x_i^2+x_j^2+2x_ix_j)^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}-(x_i^2+x_j^2-2x_ix_j)^{\frac{\alpha}{2}} &=2\sum_{m\geq 1\text{ odd}}\frac{\frac{\alpha}{2}(\frac{\alpha}{2}-1)...(\frac{\alpha}{2}-m+1)}{m!}(x_i^2+x_j^2)^{\frac{\alpha}{2}-m}(2x_ix_j)^m. \end{align*} Note that $\alpha\in(0,2]$ ensures that the coefficients are all nonnegative, so it suffices to have every $((x_i^2+x_j^2)^{\frac{\alpha}{2}-m})_{1\leq i,j\leq n}$ is positive semi-definite, which results from that \[(x_i^2+x_j^2)^{-r}=\frac{1}{\Gamma(r)}(e^{-x_i^2t}t^{(r-1)/2},e^{-x_i^2t}t^{(r-1)/2})_{L^2[0,+\infty]},\forall r>0.\]

According to the official solutions it is also true that \[\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n|x_i-x_j|^\alpha\le\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n|x_i+x_j|^\alpha\] for all $\alpha\in(0,2]$ . The above solutions work for all $\alpha\le1$ but concavity breaks for $\alpha>1$ . That case seems to require more non-elementary machinery.
We just need to generalize what @Mr.Trick has done in #58 a bit. The $\alpha=2$ case can be checked directly. Note that for $0<\alpha<2$ , the following identity holds (could be proved by, e.g. integrating by parts): \[ \int_0^\infty \frac{1-\cos(at)}{t^{1+\alpha}} \mathrm dt =\frac{\pi}{2 \Gamma(\alpha+1) \sin(\alpha \pi /2)} |a|^\alpha. \] Therefore, \begin{align*} |a+b|^\alpha-|a-b|^\alpha &=\frac{2 \Gamma(\alpha+1) \sin(\alpha \pi /2)}{\pi} \int_0^\infty \frac{\cos((a-b)t-\cos((a+b)t)}{t^{1+\alpha}} \mathrm dt & =\frac{2 \Gamma(\alpha+1) \sin(\alpha \pi /2)}{\pi} \int_0^\infty \frac{2\sin(at)\sin(bt)}{t^{1+\alpha}} \mathrm dt \end{align*} Hence \begin{align*} \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \left( |x_i+x_j|^\alpha-|x_i-x_j|^\alpha \right) & =\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{2 \Gamma(\alpha+1) \sin(\alpha \pi /2)}{\pi} \int_0^\infty \frac{2\sin(x_it)\sin(x_jt)}{t^{1+\alpha}} \mathrm dt &=\frac{4 \Gamma(\alpha+1) \sin(\alpha \pi /2)}{\pi} \int_0^\infty \frac{(\sum_{i=1}^n \sin(x_it) )^2}{t^{1+\alpha}} \mathrm dt \ge 0. \end{align*} The equality holds when $\sum_{i=1}^n \sin(x_it)$ is identical $0$ , which easily implies $\{ x_1,\ldots,x_n \}=\{ -x_1,\ldots,-x_n \}$ .

Note that for $0<\alpha<2$ , the following identity holds (could be proved by, e.g. integrating by parts): \[ \int_0^\infty \frac{1-\cos(at)}{t^{1+\alpha}} \mathrm dt =\frac{\pi}{2 \Gamma(\alpha+1) \sin(\alpha \pi /2)} |a|^\alpha. \] Therefore, \begin{align*} |a+b|^\alpha-|a-b|^\alpha &=\frac{2 \Gamma(\alpha+1) \sin(\alpha \pi /2)}{\pi} \int_0^\infty \frac{\cos((a-b)t-\cos((a+b)t)}{t^{1+\alpha}} \mathrm dt & =\frac{2 \Gamma(\alpha+1) \sin(\alpha \pi /2)}{\pi} \int_0^\infty \frac{2\sin(at)\sin(bt)}{t^{1+\alpha}} \mathrm dt \end{align*}
This identity (also observed by Sangchul Lee in the link in #49) is very cool and immediately kills the problem.

With this failure experience, I will try to make the motivation for each step as clear as possible. Also, the motivation for the steps would make clear sense to those who have attempted the problem at least twice or thrice.

<details><summary>First Step</summary>Ok so, now we want to start with a key idea in mind. Surely, if you have tried this problem at least once, a very natural idea would be induction of course. But, we don't know how to construct our inductive argument very naturally. Note that normal manipulations and straightforward induction wouldn't work. So we try to reverse induct, i.e. we try to impose a condition such that the original inequality on \(n\) variables becomes an inequality on \(n-1\) variables and keep iterating it to get a trivial inequality in one variable. But, we also need to make sure that if that condition is not true, we would actually show that it suffices to show for this particular condition to be true. We discuss more about this condition in the next step.</details>

<details><summary>Second Step</summary>Rewrite the inequality as \[\sum_{i=1}^n\sqrt{2|x_i|}+2\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}\sqrt{|x_i+x_j|}\geq2\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}\sqrt{|x_i-x_j|}\] So, we want to impose a condition so that one of the \(\sqrt{2x_i}\) term cancels out, and all terms in the sums involving \(\sqrt{|x_i+x_j|}\) and \(\sqrt{|x_i-x_j|}\) lose a variable. Now, if we get a condition so that there is a pair \((i,j)\) and a \(k\) for which \(\sqrt{|x_i-x_j|}=\sqrt{2|x_k|}\) holds, we are close. Note that if we impose \(x_i+x_j=0\) for a pair \((i,j)\) then this condition holds and surprisingly, we get our desired condition! Now we have to show that if \(x_i+x_j\neq 0\) then it nails down to the scenario where \(x_i+x_j=0\) and then we're done. For details, please see the next step!!</details>

<details><summary>Third Step</summary>If you have tried this problem for a while, you would have done quite a lot of manipulations. So, it wouldn't be shocking for you to understand this step. So basically I am going to translate the full sequence \(x_i\) with a \(k\), note clearly that the right hand side remains unchanged. We rewrite the left hand side as \[\sum_{i,j}\sqrt{|x_i-x_j|}\] Now, notice that for sufficiently small \(\alpha
\) by Jensen, \[\sum_{i,j}\sqrt{|x_i+x_j-2\alpha|}+\sum_{i,j}\sqrt{|x_i+x_j-2\alpha|}\leq \sum_{i,j}2\sqrt{|x_i+x_j|}\] so it means that \(\sum_{i,j}\sqrt{|x_i+x_j\pm2\alpha|}\leq\sum_{i,j}\sqrt{|x_i+x_j|}\) so we can choose our desired \(k\). We could keep translating this sequence until you reach a point where there exists a pair \((i,j)\) so that \(x_i+x_j=0\). It now suffices to show that the inequality holds for \(x_i+x_j=0\).</details>

<details><summary>Fourth and Final Step</summary>Finally, we are about to end this problem, we know that if \(x_i+x_j=0\), then the problem reduces to \(n-1\) variables. And similarly, it suffices to show that in the \(n-1\) variable inequality if the sum of any two of them is zero we're done and we can keep digging in and finally reach our destination, that is the problem just burns down to two variables. I guess the proof for the \(n=2\) case is quite easy, so I'll leave it for you guys to work on it, and yeah! We're done!!!!</details>

We have to prove  $$  \displaystyle f(x_1,\dots,x_n):= \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \sqrt{|x_i+x_j|} - \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \sqrt{|x_i-x _j|}\ge 0 \qquad (1) $$  	
Consider a matrix  $ A$  with entries  $ a_{ij},1\le i,j\le n$  where   $$  a_{ij}= \sqrt{|x_i+x_j|} -  \sqrt{|x_i-x_j|} . $$  Then  $$  f(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\mathbf{e}^TA\mathbf{e}\qquad(2) $$  where  $ \mathbf{e}$  is the vector in  $ \mathbb{R}^n$  with all coordinates equal to  $ 1$  and  $ \mathbf{e}^T$  is the transpose matrix of the vertical vector  $ \mathbf{e}$ . So, we must prove the right hand side of  $ (2)$  is not negative. In fact, something more general holds  $$   \mathbf{v}^TA\mathbf{v} \ge 0, \forall \mathbf{v}\in \mathbb{R}^n \qquad(3) $$  Note that the matrix  $ A$  is symmetric. Thus, we have to prove  $ A$  is positive semidefinite, which (by definition) means  $ A$  is symmetric and satisfies  $ (3)$ . In order to prove that  $ A$  is positive semidefinite, it is enough to show that there is an inner product vector space  $ X$  (over  $ \mathbb{R}$ ) and vectors  $ f_i\in X, i=1,2,\dots,n$  such that  $ a_{ij}=\langle f_i,f_j\rangle,$  that is,  $ A$  is the Gram matrix of some  $ n$  vectors in  $ X.$  Let us consider the following family of functions  $$  \displaystyle f_a(x):=\frac{\sin ax}{x^{3/4}} $$  where  $ a\in \mathbb{R}$  is a parameter. Clearly,  $ f_a(x)\in L^2(0,\infty), \forall a\in\mathbb{R}$  since  $ f_a$  is continuous in  $ (0,\infty)$ ,  $ \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0}f_a(x)=0$  and  $ \displaystyle \int_1^{\infty} f_a(x)^2\,dx\le  \int_1^{\infty} x^{-3/2}\,dx<\infty. $  Let us calculate  $$  \displaystyle \langle f_a,f_b\rangle=\int_0^{\infty}f_a(x)f_b(x)\,dx $$  We have  $$  \displaystyle  \langle f_a,f_b\rangle  = \int_0^{\infty}\frac{\sin ax\sin bx}{x^{3/2}}\,dx=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\cos(a-b)x- \cos(a+b)x }{x^{3/2}}\,dx \qquad(4) $$  We cannot represent the above expression as difference of two integrals because  $ \displaystyle \int_0^A \frac{\cos \lambda x}{x^{3/2}}\,dx$  is not convergent in any neighborhood of  $ 0$  while the difference of the two cosines as in  $ (4)$  is. So, we use the following trick to separate the two cosine terms  $$  \displaystyle  \langle f_a,f_b\rangle  = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\infty}\frac{1-\cos(a+b)x}{x^{3/2}}\,dx- \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\infty}\frac{1-\cos(a-b)x}{x^{3/2}}\,dx  $$  Let  $ \displaystyle I_{\lambda}:= \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\infty}\frac{1-\cos\lambda x}{x^{3/2}}\,dx .$  By changing variable  $ u=|\lambda|x$  we get  $$  \displaystyle I_{\lambda}=\sqrt{|\lambda|}  \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\infty}\frac{1-\cos u}{u^{3/2}}\,du = c \sqrt{|\lambda|}  $$  where  $ c$  is some positive constant. Thus, it yields  $$  \displaystyle  \langle f_a,f_b\rangle =c\left( \sqrt{|a+b|}-\sqrt{|a-b|}\right) $$  Therefore  $ \displaystyle a_{ij}=\frac{1}{c}\langle f_{x_i},f_{x_j}\rangle.$ To recap. Our matrix  $ A$  turns out to be the Gram matrix (multiplied by a positive constant  $ 1/c$ ) of the vectors  $ f_{x_i}\in L^2(0,\infty), i=1,2,\dots,n.$  So,  $ A$  is positive semidefinite.

I did the same as few others above, a different calculus-based approach for $n = 2$ base case I took instead of $n = 0$ base case :blush: For base case $n = 2$ , we have to prove that $$ 2\sqrt{|x_1 - x_2|} \leq 2\sqrt{|x_1 + x_2|} + \sqrt{|2x_1|} + \sqrt{|2x_2|}. $$ We observe that the inequality is trivial when at $\text{sgn}(x_1) = \text{sgn}(x_2)$ , therefore we take $x_1$ non-negative and $x_2$ non-positive, with $x_3 = -x_2$ . The inequality transforms to proving that $$ 2\sqrt{x_1 + x_3} - 2\sqrt{x_1 - x_3} \leq \sqrt{2x_1} + \sqrt{2x_3}, $$ where we assume $x_1 \geq x_3$ without loss of generality. Then squaring both sides gives $$ 8x_1 - 8\sqrt{x_1^2 - x_3^2} \leq 2x_1 + 2x_3 + 4\sqrt{x_1x_3} \implies 3x_1 \leq x_3 + 2\sqrt{x_1x_3} + 4\sqrt{x_1^2 - x_3^2}. $$ Plugging in $x_3 = kx_1$ for $k \in [0, 1]$ , we see that we need to prove that $f(k) = k - 3 + 2\sqrt{k} + 4\sqrt{1-k^2} \geq 0$ for all $k \in [0, 1]$ . We see that $f$ is continuous and double differentiable in this interval (not hard to verify) and $f''(x) = \dfrac{-1}{2 x^{3/2}} - \dfrac{4}{(1 - x^2)^{3/2}}$ which is always negative for $x \in [0, 1]$ , implying that $f$ is continuous and concave in $[0, 1]$ . Since $f(0) = 1$ and $f(1) = 0$ , we see that $f(k)$ must be non-negative for $k \in [0, 1]$ , as desired. Remark: IMHO I dunno what I did for this base case. Here is a version of the integral solution with a bit of motivation for the "magic identity" in the second solution above.
The igniting spark is the identity
\[\int_0^{\infty} \frac{f(cx)}{x^{\alpha}} dx=c^{\alpha-1} \int_0^{\infty} \frac{f(t)}{t^{\alpha}} dt\]
for an arbitrary function  $f$  under the sole condition that both integrals are convergent. Indeed, this follows immediately from the variable substitution  $t=c\alpha$ : The point of this identity is that it allows us to express the function  $c^{\alpha-1}$  (up to the constant factor on the RHS) as an integral over  $f(cx)$ . Indeed, specialising to  $\alpha=\frac{3}{2}$  we find that
\[\sqrt{\vert c\vert}=\frac{1}{C_f} \int_0^{\infty} \frac{f(cx)}{x^{3/2}} dx\]
for an arbitrary even function  $f:\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$  which is non-negative and not identically zero and for which  $C_f=\int_0^{\infty} \frac{f(t)}{t^{3/2}} dt$  exists (e.g. this is the case when  $f$  is bounded and vanishes at  $0$  to order at least two).
It thus completely suffices to find such a function  $f$  for which we can prove the inequality
\[\sum_{i,j=1}^n f(x_i-x_j) \le \sum_{i,j=1}^n f(x_i+x_j).\]
Note that for  $f(x)=\sqrt{\vert x\vert}$ , this is just the original problem, but we have gained a lot of extra flexibility since we are now allowed to choose  $f$ , under only mild restrictions.
Indeed, taking into account the addition formulas for trig functions, one can now come up with the choice  $f(t)=1-\cos(t)$ .
This certainly satisfies the technical conditions above (the shift by  $1$  done so that the condition at  $t=0$  is satisfied, but not changing the inequality) and we see that
\[f(x_i+x_j)-f(x_i-x_j)=\cos(x_i-x_j)-\cos(x_i+x_j)=2\sin(x_i)\sin(x_j)\]
so that summing over  $i,j$  we get
\[RHS-LHS=2\sum_{i,j} \sin(x_i)\sin(x_j)=\left(\sum_i \sin(x_i)\right)^2 \ge 0\]
in our desired inequality.
(Note that the exact value of  $C_f$  can be computed, but is completely irrelevant to the argument and would only make it look more complicated than it is.)

<details><summary>Proof</summary>It is easy to see that as  $t \to \pm\infty, f(x_1+t, ..., x_n+t) \to +\infty$ , so global minima exist. Let  $\Omega$  be the circumcircle of the triangle  $A I C$ . The extension of  $B A$  beyond  $A$  meets  $\Omega$  at  $X$ , and the extension of  $B C$  beyond  $C$  meets  $\Omega$  at  $Z$ . The extensions of  $A D$  and  $C D$  beyond  $D$  meet  $\Omega$  at  $Y$  and  $T$ , respectively. Prove that \[A D+D T+T X+X A=C D+D Y+Y Z+Z C.\]

*Proposed by Dominik Burek, Poland and Tomasz Ciesla, Poland*
solution_md: <details><summary>complex bash</summary>Identify  $\Gamma$  with the unit circle, and rename  $I$  to  $J$  to avoid confusion with the imaginary unit. Let  $\Gamma$  touch  $AB, BC, CD, DA$  at  $P, Q, R, S$  respectively, and let  $O$  be the center of  $\Omega$ . We find  $$ j=0 $$    $$ |p|=|q|=|r|=|s|=1 $$    $$ a=\frac{2ps}{p+s} $$    $$ b=\frac{2pq}{p+q} $$    $$ c=\frac{2qr}{q+r} $$    $$ d=\frac{2rs}{r+s} $$    $$ o = \frac{ac(\overline{a}-\overline{c})}{\overline{a}c-a\overline{c}} = \frac{2pqrs(p+s-q-r)}{(p+s)(q+r)(ps-qr)} $$    $$ x = 2p + o - p^2\overline{o} - a = \frac{2pqr(p+s-q-r)}{(q+r)(ps-qr)} $$    $$ z = 2q + o - q^2\overline{o} - c = \frac{2pqs(p+s-q-r)}{(p+s)(ps-qr)} $$    $$ y = 2s + o - s^2\overline{o} - a = \frac{2qrs(p+s-q-r)}{(q+r)(ps-qr)} $$    $$ t = 2r + o - r^2\overline{o} - c = \frac{2prs(p+s-q-r)}{(p+s)(ps-qr)} $$  Assuming quadrilateral  $PQRS$  is positively oriented, we find  $$ |a-d| = \frac{a-d}{is} = -\frac{2is(p-r)}{(p+s)(r+s)} $$    $$ |d-t| = -\frac{d-t}{ir} = -\frac{2is(p-r)(pr-qs)}{(p+s)(r+s)(ps-qr)} $$    $$ |t-x| = \frac{|p+s-q-r||pq-rs|}{|p+s||q+r||ps-qr|} $$    $$ |x-a| = -\frac{x-a}{ip} = \frac{2i(p^2qr+2pqrs-pq^2r-pqr^2+qrs^2-pqs^2-prs^2)}{(p+s)(q+r)(ps-qr)} $$  The other four lengths are found by transposing the coordinates  $p\leftrightarrow q$ ,  $r\leftrightarrow s$ , and  $i\leftrightarrow -i$ . Doing this, we see in fact that  $TX = YZ$ , which is fortunate because there isn't an obvious vector on the unit circle perpendicular to  $t-x$  like there is for the other three sides. So it remains to show that  $$ |a-d| + |d-t| + |x-a| = |c-d| + |d-y| + |z-c| $$  Indeed, we compute  $$ |a-d| + |d-t| = -\frac{2is(p-q)(p-r)}{(p+s)(ps-qr)} $$  and so  $$ |a-d| + |d-t| + |x-a| = \frac{2i(p^2qr+pq^2s+pr^2s+qrs^2+4pqrs-p^2qs-p^2rs-pq^2r-q^2rs-pqr^2-qr^2s-pqs^2-prs^2)}{(p+s)(q+r)(ps-qr)} $$  This is indeed symmetric under the transposition  $p\leftrightarrow q$ ,  $r\leftrightarrow s$ , and  $i\leftrightarrow -i$ , so we are done.  $\blacksquare$</details>

Let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle of the triangle $A I C$ . The extension of $B A$ beyond $A$ meets $\Omega$ at $X$ , and the extension of $B C$ beyond $C$ meets $\Omega$ at $Z$ . The extensions of $A D$ and $C D$ beyond $D$ meet $\Omega$ at $Y$ and $T$ , respectively. Prove that \[A D+D T+T X+X A=C D+D Y+Y Z+Z C.\]

After  $XT=YX$ , we need to prove that  $AD+DT+XA=CD+DY+ZC$ .  $AD-CD+DT+XA=DY+ZC$ . Use Pitot,  $AD-CD=AB-BC$ , and we have that,  $AB+DT+XA=BC+DY+ZC$ . $BX+DT=BZ+DY$ .  $BX-BZ=DY-DT$ .
Note that, $BX-BY=\frac{(BC-BA)BZ}{BA}$  and that  $DY-DT=\frac{(DC-DA)DT}{DA}$ . Since,  $AD-CD=AB-BC$ , suffices to show that  $\frac{DT}{DA}=\frac{BZ}{BA}$ .
To show this we proceed as follows: $\frac{DT}{DA}=\frac{sin\angle DAT}{sin\angle DTA}=\frac{sin\angle XAZ}{sin\angle AZC}=\frac{sin\angle ZAB}{sin\angle AZB}=\frac{BZ}{BA}$ .

Inverting around  $\Gamma$ ,  $A',C',X',Y',Z',T'$  are all collinear. Let  $S,V,W,U$  be the tangencies  of  $\Gamma$  with  $AD, DC, CB, BA$ . Note that  $D',C',T'\in (IV)$ ;  $X',A',B'\in (IU)$ ;  $Z',C',B'\in (IW)$ ;  $A',D',Y'\in (IS)$ .  $$ \measuredangle IZ'T'=\measuredangle IZ'C'=\measuredangle IWC'=\measuredangle C'VI=\measuredangle C'T'I=\measuredangle Z'T'I $$  Hence,  $IZ'=IT'$ , equivalently  $IZ=IT$ . Similarly,  $IY=IX$  Now, \[A D+D T+T X+X A=C D+D Y+Y Z+Z C\] is equivalent to 
\[D V+A U+D T+T X+X A=CW+DS+D Y+Y Z+Z C\] or \[VT+TX+XU=WZ+ZY+YS\]. Which is true since  $VT=WZ$ ,  $TX=ZY$ ,  $XU=YS$ .

First, we claim that: **Claim:** $XYZT$ is an isosceles trapezoid. *Proof:* Observe that $AI$ is the angle bisector of $\angle BAD \equiv \angle XAY$ , so $IX=IY$ . Similarly, $IZ=IT$ , so $XY\parallel ZT$ . This gives the claim. $\blacksquare$ In particular, the claim implies that $XT=YZ$ , removing two terms in the equation to be proved. Now, here is the critical observation, if we let the $\Gamma$ touches $AB, AD, CB, CD$ at $P,Q,R,S$ , respectively, then $\triangle IPX\cong\triangle IQY$ (as $IP=IQ$ and $IX=IY$ ). Thus, $PX=QY$ . Similarly, $RZ=ST$ . Therefore \begin{align*} PX + ST &= QY + RZ (AX + AP) + (DT + DS) &= (DY + QD) + (RC + CZ) (AX + DT) + (AP + DS) &= (DY + CZ) + (QD + RC) (AX + DT) + (AQ + QD) &= (DY + CZ) + (DS + SC) AX + DT + AD &= DY + CZ + DC, \end{align*} done.

As before, from  $IX=IY$  and  $IT=IZ$  we obtain  $TY=XZ$ .
Hence, it suffices to show that  $AD+DT+AX=CD+DY+CZ$ .
From  $\triangle ADC \sim \triangle TDY$  and  $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle ZBX$  we get  $$ \frac{AD}{DT} = \frac{CD}{DY} = \frac{AC}{TY} = \frac{AC}{XZ} = \frac{BC}{BA+AX} = \frac{AB}{BC+CZ}. $$  Now we can express everything in terms of the quadrilateral  $ABCD$  and the length  $XZ$ :  $$ CZ = \frac{AB \cdot XZ}{BC} - BC, \quad AX = \frac{BC \cdot XZ}{AC} - AB, \quad DY = \frac{CD \cdot XZ}{AC}, \quad DT = \frac{AD \cdot XZ}{AC}. $$  Plugging in, the claim reduces to  $$ AD + \frac{AD \cdot XZ}{AC} + \frac{BC \cdot XZ}{AC} - AB = CD + \frac{CD \cdot XZ}{AC} + \frac{AB \cdot XZ}{AC} - BC, $$  which follows directly from  $AB+CD=BC+AD$ .

Let  $\Gamma$  be tangent to  $AB, BC, CD$  and  $DA$  at  $P$ ,  $Q$ ,  $R$  and  $S$ , respectively. After showing that  $IX=IY$ ,  $IT=IZ$  and  $XT=YZ$ , it amounts to prove that
\[XP+DT=QZ+DY.\]
However, if the inradius is  $r$  this can be computed as follows:
\begin{align*}
XP+DT &= \sqrt{IX^2-r^2}+\sqrt{IT^2-r^2}-DR
&= \sqrt{IY^2-r^2} + \sqrt{IZ^2-r^2} - DS
&= QZ + DY
\end{align*}

I find this problem interesting, and strange at the same time. Anyways, here is my solution: **Claim 1:** $ZY=XT$ *Proof:* Consider $O$ the center of $\Omega$ and $IO\cap \Omega =\{ I'\}.$ $\angle BAI=\angle DAI\Rightarrow AI$ is the exterrnal bisector of $\angle XAY$ . On the other hand, $\angle IAI'=90^o\Rightarrow AI'$ is the internal bisector of $\angle XAY\Rightarrow I'$ is the midpoint of the arc $XY$ not containing $I\Rightarrow IX=IY.$ Similarly, $IZ=IT$ . Now combining these 2 equalities, we get $ZY=XT$ . $\blacksquare$ We are left to prove that $AD+DT+XA= CD+DY+ZC$ . **Claim 2:** $\frac{DY}{DC}=\frac{BZ}{BA}$ *Proof:* $$ \frac{BZ}{BA}=\frac{XZ}{AC}=\frac{TY}{AC}=\frac{DY}{DC} $$ because $BA\cdot BX=BC\cdot BZ$ and $TYCA$ is cyclic with $\{ D\}=TC\cap AY$ . $\blacksquare$ Now all he have to do is to use Pitot theorem for the quadrilateral $ABCD$ ( $BC+AD=DC+AB$ ). $$ \frac{DY}{DC}=\frac{BZ}{BA}\Leftrightarrow DY\cdot \frac{AB-BC}{DC}=BZ\cdot \frac{AB-BC}{BA}\Leftrightarrow $$ $$ \Leftrightarrow DY\cdot \frac{DA-DC}{DC}=BZ\cdot \frac{AB-BC}{BA}\Leftrightarrow DY\cdot \frac{DA}{DC}+ZB\cdot \frac{BC}{BA}=DY+BZ\Leftrightarrow $$ $$ \Leftrightarrow DY\cdot \frac{DT}{DY}+ZB\cdot \frac{XB}{ZB}=DY+BZ\Leftrightarrow DT+XB=DY+BZ\Leftrightarrow $$ $$ \Leftrightarrow DT+XB+AD-AB=DY+BZ+CD-BC\Leftrightarrow AD+DT+XA=CD+DY+ZC $$ and the problem is finished.

--------------**Claim.** We have that  $XT=YZ$ .

We have that 

\begin{align*}\angle TIX&=\angle AIC-\angle XIA-\angle TIC
&=\angle AIC-\angle IAB+\angle IXA-\angle ICB+\angle ITC
&=\angle AIC-\angle IAB+\angle ICA-\angle ICB+\angle IAC
&= 180-\angle ICB-\angle IAB
\end{align*}
which is symmetric in  $A$  and  $C$ , so  $\widehat{XT}=\widehat{YZ}$ . This also gives an isosceles trapezoid.  $\blacksquare$ ---------
Now, it suffices to show that  $AD+DT+XA= CD+DY +ZC$ . By Pitot, this is equivalent to  $BX+DT = BZ+DY$ . Finally, we write (by Law of Sines in  $\triangle TDY$  and  $\triangle XBZ$ , and using the equal diagonals of the isosceles trapezoid)
\begin{align*}&BX+DT = BZ+DY
\impliedby& \frac 1 {\sin \angle D}\cdot (\sin \angle TYD-\sin \angle YTD) + \frac{1}{\sin \angle B}\cdot (\sin \angle BZX -\sin \angle BXZ)=0
\impliedby& \frac 1 {\sin \angle D}\cdot (\sin \angle DCA-\sin \angle DAC) + \frac{1}{\sin \angle B}\cdot (\sin \angle CAB -\sin \angle ACB)=0
\impliedby& (DA-DC) + (BC-AB) = 0\end{align*}
where the last step follows from Law of Sines in  $\triangle ADC$  and  $\triangle ABC$ .

Thus we are done by Pitot.  $\blacksquare$

Denote the half-angles at  $A,B,C,D$  to be  $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\theta$ . Then,  $\textbf{Claim 1: }$ .
\[\frac12(AC) = (\angle ICT +\angle IAZ + \angle ADC - 180)= \gamma + \alpha + 2\theta-180.\] 
Thus, 
\[(TX)=2\angle APC - (AC) = 2\cdot (\angle BAD + \angle ADC - 180)-2(\gamma+\alpha+2\theta-180)=2(\alpha-\gamma)\]
Similarly, we get  $(ZY)=2(\alpha-\gamma)$ , so we have that  $TX=ZY$ . $\square$  $\textbf{Claim 2: }$ .
\[\frac{DY}{DC} = \frac{\sin(TCY)}{\sin(\angle CYA)} = \frac{\sin(\angle BCD+\angle ZCY)}{\sin(\angle AIC)}=\frac{\sin(\alpha+\gamma)}{\sin(\angle AIC)}\]
\[\frac{BX}{BC}=\frac{\sin(\angle BCT+\angle TCX)}{\sin(AXC)} =\frac{\sin(\alpha +\gamma )}{\sin(\angle AIC)}\]
Thus,  $\frac{BX}{BC}=\frac{DY}{DC}$ , so we have
\[\frac{Pow(B)}{Pow(D)}=\frac{BA\cdot BX}{DY\cdot AD} = \frac{BA\cdot BC}{DA\cdot DC}\] $\square$ Now, note that using Claim 1, and by Pitot's, since  $AD+BC=AB+CD$ , we have
\[\Longrightarrow AD+DT+XA = CD+DY+ZC \Leftrightarrow AB+DT+XA=BC+DY+ZC\]
Combining lengths
\[BX+DT = BZ + DY\Longleftrightarrow \frac{Pow(B)}{AB}+\frac{Pow(D)}{CD}=\frac{Pow(B)}{BC}+\frac{Pow(D)}{AD}\]
Which by applying Claim 2 gives  $BC+AD=BA+DC$  and we're done.  $\blacksquare$ .

Let the incircle of  $ABCD$  touch sides  $AB,BC,CD,DA$  at  $E,F,G,H$ , respectively. We'll start by proving the following claim:**Claim:**  $\triangle XIY$  and  $\triangle TIZ$  are isosoclece with  $IX=IY$  and  $IT=IZ$ , respectively.  
*Proof.* Angle chasing. Observe  $\measuredangle IXY=\measuredangle IAY=\measuredangle IAD=\measuredangle BAI=\measuredangle XAI=\measuredangle XYI$  so  $\triangle XIY$  is isosolece with  $IX=IY$ . Similar work shows that  $\triangle TIZ$  is also isosocles with  $IT-IZ$ .  $\square$ An immediate consequence of this claim is that  $TX=YZ$ , so it now suffices to show that   $$ AD+DT+XA=CD+DY+ZC. $$   By Pitot,  $AD+BC=AB+CD \iff AD=AB+CD-BC$  so the desired equation can be rewritten as 

\begin{align*}AD+DT+XA=CD+DY+ZC&\iff (AB+\cancel{CD}-BC)+DT+XA=\cancel{CD}+DY+ZC&\iff AB+DT+XA=BC+DY+ZC&\iff (AE+\cancel{EB})+DT+XA=(\cancel{BF}+FC)+DY+ZC&\iff (AE+XA)+DT=(FC+ZC)+DY&\iff EX+DT=FZ+DY &\iff EX+(DT+DG)=FZ+(DY+DH) &\iff EX+GT=FZ+HY \end{align*} with the second-to-last line coming from the fact that  $DG=DH$ . 

To finish, note that  $\triangle IEX\cong IHY$  and  $\triangle IGT\cong \triangle IFZ$  which gives us  $EX=HY$  and  $GT=FZ$ , as required.  $\blacksquare$ .

This is 38 days late but nevertheless here is my solution from the competition.  $\textbf{Lemma 1:}$   $TX = YZ$   $\textbf{Proof)}$  
Let  $BC$  and  $AD$  intersect at  $U$ , then notice that   $$ \angle CUY = \angle UBA + \angle BAU = \angle CBA + \angle DAB  $$   and also that   $$ \angle UYC = \angle AYC = 180^{\circ} - \angle AIC = \angle ABC + \frac{\angle BAD + \angle BCD}{2} $$  Therefore   $$ \angle ZCY = \angle UCY = 180^{\circ} - \angle UYC - \angle CUY = \frac{\angle BCD - \angle BAC}{2} = \angle TAX $$   by symmetry proving the desired claim.  $\square$  

Now, notice that we have to prove that   $$ AD+DT+XA = CD+DY+ZC $$   which by Pitot is equivalent to proving that   $$ BX+DT = DY+BZ $$   $\textbf{Lemma 2:}$    $$ \frac{BZ}{BA} = \frac{BX}{BC} = \frac{DY}{DC} = \frac{DT}{DA} $$   $\textbf{Proof)}$  
Notice that the first and the last equality follow by PoP. 
On the other hand notice that   $$ \frac{BX}{BC} = \frac{\sin \angle BCX}{\sin \angle BXC} = \frac{\sin \angle XCZ}{\sin \angle AXC} = \frac{\sin \angle TCY}{\sin \angle AYC} = \frac{\sin \angle DCY}{\sin \angle DYC} = \frac{DY}{DC} $$   which proves the middle equality as well.   $\square$  

Now, let the ratio in  $\textbf{Lemma 2}$  be  $r$ . Then, multiplying Pitot by  $r$  gives us that  $BX + DT = DY + BZ$ , as desired.  $\blacksquare$

Similarly, the angle bisector of  $\angle TCZ$  passes through  $I'$ . Since arcs  $XY$  and  $TZ$  both share a midpoint of  $I'$ , it follows that  $XT = YZ$ , so it suffices to show that
\[ XA + AD + DT = ZC + CD + DY.\]
Letting  $f(P)$  denote the length of the tangent from  $P$  to  $\Gamma$ , we can rewrite the LHS and RHS of the above equation to
\[ f(X) + f(T) = f(Y) + f(Z).\]
Because  $I$  is the midpoint of arcs  $XY$  and  $TZ$ ,  $f(X) = f(Y)$  and  $f(T) = f(Z)$ , so the above equation is true.

Let  $EF\cap BC=P$ ,  $AD\cap BC=D_0$ ,  $(XED)\cap (ADC)=\{ D,Q\}$  and  $N\in (ADC)$  such that  $DN\parallel BC$ .**Lemma 1:**  $PD$  is tangent to  $(BDC)$  at  $D$ .
<details><summary>Proof</summary>The condition implies that  $ED$  is tangent to  $(DD_0C)$  at  $D$ , so we have  $\angle DD_0C=\angle EDC$ . Now, for  $\angle (DF,DB)$  (the clockwise angle between the lines  $DF$  and  $DB$ ), we have  $\angle (DF,DB)=\angle FDA+\angle D_0DB=\angle DBD_0+\angle D_0DB=\angle DD_0C=\angle EDC$ . This means that the lines  $DB$  and  $DC$  are isogonal in  $\angle FDE$ , so by the Isogonal Lines Lemma, we get  $FB\cap EC=A$ ,  $EF\cap BC=P$   $\rightarrow$   $DA$  and  $DP$  are isogonal in  $\angle FDE$ , so  $\angle CDP=\angle ADF=\angle CBD$ .  $ \square$</details>**Lemma 2:**  $X,Q$  and  $N$  are collinear.
*(The proof is just by angle chasing)*

Now, to finish the proof of the problem, we need to prove that  $P$  lies on  $O_1O_2$  or, equivalently, that  $PD=PQ$ . Note that because of Lemma 1, the circle with center  $P$  and radius  $PD$  is in fact the  $D$ -Apollonian circle of  $\triangle BDC$ , so we want to prove that  $\frac{BQ}{QC}=\frac{BD}{DC}$ . We accomplish this by way of two inversions. To start, invert about  $D$  with arbitrary radius.**<u>First Inversion</u>**
*Placement of points:*
 
- $D$  is on the interior of  $\triangle ABC$ , satisfying  $\angle ABD=\angle DCA$
- $X$  lies on  $(ADC)$  such that  $x\neq D$  and  $\frac{BX}{XC}=\frac{BD}{DC}$  (i.e.  $X$  lies on the  $D$ -Apollonian circle of  $\triangle BDC$ )
- $N$  is the intersection of  $AC$  and the tangent at  $D$  to  $(BDC)$
- $Q$  lies on  $AC$  such that  $D$ ,  $X$ ,  $N$  and  $Q$  are concyclic
[/list]

*Want to prove:*  $BQ=QC$ We now perform a second inversion, this time centered at  $C$  and with arbitrary radius.**<u>Doubly-inverted Diagram</u>**
*Placement of points:*
[list]
- $D$  is on the exterior of  $\triangle ABC$ , on the opposite side of  $AB$  as  $C$ , satisfying  $\angle BDC+\angle ACD=\angle BAC$
- $N$  lies on  $AC$  so that  $(CDN)$  is tangent to  $BD$  at the point  $D$
- $X$  lies on  $AD$  such that  $BD=BX$
- $Q$  is the second intersection of the line  $AC$  and  $(DNX)$

*Want to prove:*  $BQ=BC$ Now, let  $(CDN)$  intersect  $CB$  for the second time at  $J$  and let  $JN\cap AB=K$ . We have that   $$ \angle CDN=180^{\circ}-\angle DNC-\angle NCD=180^{\circ}-\angle BDC-\angle ACD=180^{\circ}-\angle BAC $$   so   $$ \angle CJK=\angle CJN=180^{\circ}-\angle BAC \rightarrow (ACJK) $$  . 

Furthermore,   $$ \frac{BD}{BK}=\frac{BD^2}{BD\cdot BK}=\frac{BJ\cdot BC}{BD\cdot BK}=\frac{BA\cdot BK}{BD\cdot BK}=\frac{BA}{BD} $$   and  $\angle  KBD=\angle ABD$ , so   $$ \triangle ABD\sim \triangle DBK\rightarrow \angle DKB=\angle BDA\equiv\angle BDX=\angle DXB\rightarrow (DXKB) $$  .

Now, we have that  $(DXKB)$  and  $(DNXQ)$ , so  $AB\cdot AK=AX\cdot AD=AN\cdot AQ$ , hence  $(BKQN)$ . This means that  $\angle CQB\equiv \angle AQB=\angle NKA=180^{\circ}-\angle AJK=\angle JCA\equiv \angle BCQ$ , i.e.,  $\angle CQB=\angle BCQ$ , which immediately implies that  $BC=BQ$ , as desired. $\blacksquare$

OHMYGOD, This is my problem. I'm quite surprised to see it on IMO. I even doubted that this problem will be on the Shortlist. The story of how I came up with it is quite lengthy, and I don't remember all the details, but I got chain of problems, each time improving former version by doing inversion, watching some new stuff in construction in Geogebra, until finally, in few months came up with the final version of this problem. I actually sent slightly different proposal, and in that statement the fact of this problem was very unexpected for me, so I decided to send it on IMO. Thanks to Fedir Yudin, who first solved this problem and to Anton Trygub who first solved it with the nice solution which I present you here.

Will make a diagram later. Let $P$ be the point where $AD$ intersects $(BDC)$ for the second time. Then $\angle APC = \angle DBC = \angle FDA$ . As $\angle FAD = \angle CAP$ it follows that $\triangle AFD \sim \triangle ACP$ , thus $AD/AP = AF/AC$ . Similarly $AE/AB = AD/AP$ , so $AB \cdot AF = AC \cdot AE$ and $BCEF$ is cyclic. Now we prove that $(DEF)$ and $(BDC)$ are tangent. Let $AD$ intersect $BC$ at $K$ , then \[\angle FED = \angle AED - \angle AEF = \angle ABP - \angle ABC = \angle PBC = \angle KDC\] Now $\angle FED + \angle DCB = \angle DKB$ and some more easy angle chasing shows $\angle DKB = \angle FDB$ , so these circumcircles are indeed tangent. Let $EF$ and $BC$ intersect at $T$ , then $T$ is the radical center of $(DEF)$ , $(DBC)$ and $(BCEF)$ , so $D$ lies on the circle $\Omega$ with center $T$ that is orthogonal to $(BCEF)$ . To finish it is enough to prove that the second intersection of $(ADC)$ and $(XDE)$ also lies on $\Omega$ . We will actually generalize this, and prove that it holds for any point $D$ on $\Omega$ . Now we invert at $D$ , with the inverted diagram looking as follows:
Let $BCEF$ be an isosceles trapezoid with $BC \parallel EF$ and let $\Omega$ be its axis of symmetry. Let $D$ be any point on the plane, and $A$ be the second intersection of $(BDF)$ and $(CDE)$ . Let $X$ be a point on $(CDE)$ such that $BD/DC = BX/XC$ . Then $AC$ and $EX$ intersect on $\Omega$ .
Now let $P = BF \cap CE$ , then $A, D, P$ are collinear on account of $AD$ being the radical axis of $(BDF)$ and $(CDE)$ , and $P$ lies on $\Omega$ . Rewording the problem wrt the circle $(CDE)$ and relabeling points, we get the following:
Let $ABCDE$ be a cyclic pentagon, let $P = AB \cap CD$ and $Q = BD \cap CE$ , and let $X$ be the reflection of $D$ wrt $PQ$ . Then $AX/AD = EX/ED$ .
To finish, notice that the required statement is equivalent to $AX/XE = AD/DE$ , which is equivalent to $X$ lying on the $D$ -Apollonian circle of $\triangle ADE$ . Let $DD \cap AE = R$ , then by Pascal on $DDBAEC$ we get $P, Q, R$ collinear, implying that $RD = RX$ , which finishes as $R$ is the center of the Apollonian circle.

Congratulations! I really enjoyed your problem. Here goes my solution: Let $D'$ be the isogonal conjugate of $D$ with respect to $ABC$ . Since $\angle ADE=\angle DCB=\angle ACD'$ , $ED'DC$ is cyclic and similarly $FD'DB$ is cyclic. From POP we get $AE\cdot AC=AD'\cdot AD=AF\cdot AB$ therefore $BFEC$ is cyclic, too. Let $AD$ intersects $BC$ and $EF$ at $R$ and $S$ . Notice that $\angle EDC=\angle ADC-\angle ADE=\angle ADC-\angle DCB=\angle CRA\ (1)$ . Hence $$ \angle EFD+\angle DBC=\angle EFD+\angle ADF=\angle ASF=\angle CRA=\angle EDC $$ so $\odot (EDF)$ and $\odot (BDC)$ are tangent. It yields that $EF$ , $BC$ and the common internal tangent of $\odot (EDF)$ and $\odot (BDC)$ are concurrent. Let $K$ be the concurrency point. Similarly we can prove that $KD'$ is tangent to both $\odot (ED'F)$ and $\odot (BD'C)$ , so $KD'^2=KB\cdot KC=KD^2$ or $KD'=KD$ . Suppose that $\odot (EDX)$ and $\odot (ADC)$ intersects again at $P$ . We just need to prove that $K$ is the circumcenter of $\odot (PD'D)$ , since $O_1O_2$ is the perpendicular bisector of $PD$ . It's sufficient to prove that $\angle D'PD=90^\circ-\angle D'DK$ or $\angle APD'=\angle APD+\angle D'DK-90^\circ$ . Notice that $$ \angle D'DK=\angle D'DC-\angle KDC=\angle D'DC-\angle DBC=\angle D'DC-\angle ABD' $$ $$ \Longrightarrow \angle APD+\angle D'DK=\angle ACD+\angle D'DC-\angle ABD'=180-\frac12 \angle A-\angle ABD'=\angle AD'B $$ hence we need to prove that $\angle APD'=\angle AD'B-90^\circ=\angle AFD-90^\circ$ . The images of the points are denoted by primes. It's obvious that $X'$ lies on $AC$ and $\angle X'FE=180^\circ-\angle C$ . Also $P'$ lies on $D'E$ and $\odot (X'D'C)$ . We want to prove that $\angle ADP'=\angle AFD-90^\circ$ or $P'D$ passes through the circumcenter of $\odot (AFD)$ . We claim that $\triangle FX'P'\sim \triangle DRB$ . Notice that $\angle FX'E=\angle C-\angle AEF=\angle C-\angle B$ and $\angle P'X'C=\angle ED'C\overset{(1)}{=}\angle CRA$ , hence $\angle FX'P'=\angle CRA+\angle C-\angle B=\angle ARB$ . So to prove our claim we need to show that $\frac{X'F}{X'P'}=\frac{RD}{RB}$ . It's clear that $\triangle X'EP'\sim \triangle D'EC$ and $\triangle D'EC\sim \triangle RDC$ , therefore $$ \triangle X'EP'\sim \triangle RDC \Longrightarrow X'P'=X'E\cdot\frac{CR}{RD}. $$ So $$ \frac{X'F}{X'P'}=\frac{RD}{RB} \Longleftrightarrow \frac{X'F}{X'E}=\frac{RC}{RB}=\frac{AC}{AB} $$ The last equality holds by law of sines, hence the claim is proved and it yields $\angle X'P'F=\angle DBC$ . Let $J$ be the second intersection of $AC$ and $\odot (AFD)$ . We have $\angle AJF=\angle ADF=\angle DBC=\angle X'P'F$ so $X'P'JF$ is cyclic. On the other hand, we proved that $\angle P'X'C=\angle CRA=\angle B+\frac12 \angle A$ and $\angle FX'E=\angle C-\angle B$ , therefore $2\angle P'X'C+\angle FX'E=\angle A+\angle B+\angle C=180^\circ$ . It means that $X'P'$ is the external angle bisector of $\angle FX'E$ , hence $P'F=P'J$ . Also it's clear that $DF=DJ$ so $P'D$ is the perpendicular bisector of $FJ$ and passes through the circumcenter of $\odot (AFD)$ , as desired.
